lessons.title: Pressure waves, speed and wavelength
lessons.summary: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally.
lessons.body:
Everything in this module happens in air. Your synth makes a voltage; a loudspeaker turns it into moving air; a room bounces it about; an ear or a microphone turns it back into something useful. Before looking at any of those devices, you need a working model of what sound in air actually is and how it behaves with distance.

Module 1 covered decibels as ratios and dBFS, and module 5 covered dBu and dBV for signal voltages. The next lesson adds the decibel scale for *sound in air*: dB SPL.

## Sound is a pressure wave

A loudspeaker cone moving forward squashes the air in front of it slightly (an **acoustic compression**); moving back, it leaves the air slightly thinner (a **rarefaction**). Each layer of air pushes on the next, so the disturbance travels outward. The air molecules themselves only jiggle back and forth around where they started. What travels is the *pattern* of pressure.

```diagram
 cone   compression   rarefaction
  |  ||||||||    |   |   |   |||||||
  |  ||||||||    |   |   |   |||||||
  ---------> direction of travel
```

Two consequences matter for audio engineering:

- Sound is **longitudinal**: the air moves along the direction of travel, not across it.
- The pressure changes are **tiny**. Atmospheric pressure is about 101,325 Pa. A 120 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 20 Pa; a 60 dB SPL sound has an RMS pressure of 0.02 Pa. These are pressure examples, not hearing-safety thresholds.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a shove passed along a packed line of people
> Picture people standing shoulder to shoulder in a tight line. Someone at the back is nudged forward; they bump the person in front, who bumps the next, and the bump runs to the front. Nobody walks to the front of the line; each person sways forward and back.
>
> **How it maps:** The people are layers of air. A bunched-up stretch of the line is a compression, a gap is a rarefaction, and the bump moving along is the sound wave. Each person sways along the line's direction, which is what longitudinal means.
>
> **Where it stops:** Air is not a single file: the disturbance spreads out in three dimensions. Its speed is set by the air's properties, mainly temperature, not by how quickly people react, and real air molecules also move randomly at high speed all the time.

## Speed of sound

The speed of sound in air is set by the air itself, not by how loud the sound is or its pitch. In dry air it depends mainly on temperature: warmer air passes the disturbance on faster. For ideal dry air at a fixed temperature, static pressure cancels out of the sound-speed relation, so weather fronts matter much less than temperature. Humidity raises the speed a little, so precise outdoor alignment needs the actual conditions.

The working figure is **343 m/s at 20 °C**, about 1 metre every 2.9 ms. Near room temperature it changes by roughly 0.6 m/s for each degree; at 0 °C it is about 331 m/s. That speed turns up everywhere: speaker delay times, room modes, crossover alignment.

```formula reference
c ≈ 331.3 √(1 + T / 273.15)
where
c: the speed of sound in dry air, in metres per second (m/s)
T: the air temperature, in degrees Celsius (°C); everyday values are about 0–35 °C
331.3: the speed of sound in dry air at 0 °C, in m/s
273.15: the number you add to a Celsius temperature to get kelvin (absolute temperature), so 1 + T / 273.15 is the absolute temperature divided by that of 0 °C
√: square root: the number that, multiplied by itself, gives what is inside the brackets
≈: approximately equal to; the relation treats dry air as an ideal gas
In words: Sound speed in dry air rises with the square root of absolute temperature; near room temperature that is about 0.6 metres per second faster for each degree warmer, giving about 343 metres per second at 20 °C.
```

## Wavelength

**Wavelength** is how far the wave travels during one cycle. In one second sound covers about 343 m and completes as many cycles as its frequency, so each cycle covers the speed divided by the frequency. This inverse relationship is the key to the rest of the module:

```formula essential
λ = c / f
where
λ: lambda, the wavelength: the distance the wave travels during one cycle, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
f: the frequency of the sound, in hertz (Hz)
Hz: hertz, the unit of frequency: one cycle per second
In words: the wavelength is the speed of sound divided by the frequency, so doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.
```

| Frequency | Wavelength (at 343 m/s) |
|---|---|
| 20 Hz | 17.15 m |
| 100 Hz | 3.43 m |
| 1 kHz | 34.3 cm |
| 10 kHz | 3.43 cm |
| 20 kHz | 1.7 cm |

Audible wavelengths span a factor of 1,000, from longer than a house to shorter than your thumb. That is why one room, one speaker cabinet or one absorber can behave completely differently at the bottom and the top of the audio range. Relative size strongly affects diffraction and scattering; reflection and absorption also depend on material impedance, construction, mounting and incidence angle.

The same relationship applies in other media with that medium's own speed: sound in water travels about four times faster than in air, so a given frequency has a wavelength about four times longer. Frequency is set by the source; when the speed changes, the wavelength changes with it.

## Key takeaways
- Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure disturbance; molecules oscillate locally.
- Temperature changes sound speed and therefore travel time: about 343 m/s at 20 °C, about 0.6 m/s per degree.
- At a fixed sound speed, doubling frequency halves wavelength; audible wavelengths run from about 17 m to 1.7 cm.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: A 100 Hz tone in 20 °C air has a wavelength of about 3.4 m. You play the same source an octave higher, at 200 Hz, in the same room. What happens to the wavelength?

options.text: It halves, to about 1.7 m
options.explanation: Correct. At a fixed sound speed, wavelength is speed divided by frequency, so doubling the frequency halves the wavelength.

options.text: It doubles, to about 6.9 m
options.explanation: This treats wavelength as growing with frequency. Higher frequencies have shorter cycles in space, not longer ones.

options.text: It stays at 3.4 m because the air has not changed
options.explanation: The air sets the speed, not the wavelength. With the same speed, more cycles per second means each cycle covers less distance.

options.text: It halves only if the air also warms up
options.explanation: Warming the air raises the speed and lengthens wavelengths slightly; it is not needed for the octave to halve the wavelength.

questions.workedExample:
1. Wavelength is the distance sound travels during one cycle.
2. The air, and so the speed of sound (about 343 m/s), has not changed.
3. At 200 Hz the source completes twice as many cycles in each second, so each cycle must cover half the distance.
4. 3.4 m becomes about 1.7 m.

The same reasoning in reverse: an octave lower doubles the wavelength. Temperature changes the speed, which changes every wavelength a little, but that is a separate effect.

questions.prompt: You set the delay on a speaker tower 50 m from the stage assuming sound travels at 343 m/s (20 °C). The outdoor gig is at 0 °C, where sound travels at about 331 m/s, roughly 3.5 % slower. What do listeners near the tower experience?

options.text: The tower now sounds slightly late, after the stage sound
options.explanation: This gets the direction backwards. Cold air slows the stage sound, so it arrives later than you allowed for; the electrically delayed tower is now early by comparison.

options.text: The tower now sounds a few milliseconds early, before the stage sound arrives
options.explanation: Correct. The stage sound takes about 3.5 % longer than planned to cover 50 m (roughly 151 ms instead of 146 ms), so the tower leads it by about 5 ms.

options.text: The tower is tens of milliseconds early
options.explanation: That would need the speed to change by about a third. A 3.5 % change in a roughly 146 ms trip is about 5 ms.

options.text: No change: delays depend only on distance
options.explanation: Travel time depends on distance and on the speed of sound, which depends on air temperature.

questions.workedExample:
1. The tower delay is electronic: it is fixed at whatever you set, based on 343 m/s.
2. The sound from the stage travels through the cold air, about 3.5 % more slowly, so it takes about 3.5 % longer to cover the 50 m.
3. A 50 m trip at 343 m/s takes about 146 ms; 3.5 % of that is about 5 ms.
4. So the stage sound arrives about 5 ms later than you planned, and the tower plays first.

At this distance a few milliseconds affects alignment between main and delay speakers, which is why delays are set by measurement on the day.

lessons.title: Read sound pressure in dB SPL
lessons.summary: The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS.
lessons.body:
## Sound pressure level: dB SPL

Sound pressure is the changing pressure around the ambient value, measured in pascals (Pa). For a level measurement, we use its RMS value: an average size over a specified time interval. Because the range is so huge, we use decibels relative to a reference of **20 µPa** (20 millionths of a pascal), roughly the quietest 1 kHz tone a young, healthy listener can detect. The sound pressure level is:

```formula essential
L_p = 20 log_10(p / p_0)
p_0 = 20 µPa = 0.00002 Pa
where
L_p: the sound pressure level, in decibels relative to 20 µPa (dB SPL)
p: the RMS sound pressure you measure, in pascals (Pa)
p_0: the reference pressure, 20 µPa, which is defined to be 0 dB SPL
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you must raise 10 to in order to get the number, e.g. log_10(1000) = 3
µ: micro, meaning one millionth (0.000001)
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure: one newton of force per square metre
In words: count how many times bigger than 20 µPa the pressure is, take the base-10 logarithm and multiply by 20; every tenfold increase in pressure adds 20 dB.
```

The multiplier is 20, not 10, because pressure is a field quantity, like voltage: for a progressive wave in the same medium, sound intensity is proportional to pressure squared, and squaring a ratio doubles its logarithm (module 1 explains why). In practice you rarely need a calculator; a few landmarks cover most situations:

| Pressure change | Level change |
|---|---|
| × 2 | about +6 dB |
| × 10 | +20 dB |
| × 1,000,000 | +120 dB |
| ÷ 2 | about −6 dB |

| RMS pressure | Level |
|---|---|
| 20 µPa | 0 dB SPL |
| 0.02 Pa | 60 dB SPL |
| 1 Pa | about 94 dB SPL |
| 20 Pa | 120 dB SPL |

Because the scale is a ratio to a fixed reference, 0 dB SPL does not mean silence: it means "equal to 20 µPa". Quieter sounds have negative levels, and a reading only makes sense when you know the reference. A sound level meter also averages with a stated time weighting (IEC 61672-1 defines Fast, with a 125 ms time constant, and Slow, with 1 s), so Fast and Slow readings of the same music can differ.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: height above sea level
> A mountain's height is quoted "above sea level", not from the centre of the Earth. Everyone agrees on the same zero, so two heights can be compared directly, and a place below sea level simply has a negative height.
>
> **How it maps:** 20 µPa is the agreed sea level of sound pressure. A dB SPL figure tells you how far above that reference a sound is, and a level below it is negative. Without the stated reference, a bare "dB" figure is as ambiguous as a height with no zero.
>
> **Where it stops:** Height above sea level is a linear distance in metres. Decibels count *ratios* on a logarithmic scale: each extra 20 dB means ten times the pressure, not a fixed extra amount of pressure.

Remember **1 Pa ≈ 94 dB SPL**. Microphone sensitivities are quoted at 1 Pa (the microphone units) and calibrators often produce 94 dB SPL for exactly this reason.

## Key takeaways
- The air-pressure reference is 20 micropascals RMS.
- One pascal RMS is approximately 94 dB SPL.
- Pressure ratios use twenty times the base-ten logarithm.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: A sound level meter reads 94 dB SPL (an RMS pressure of 1 Pa). The source is turned up until the RMS pressure is exactly twice as large. What will the meter read?

options.text: About 97 dB SPL
options.explanation: This uses the power rule (10 log), where doubling adds 3 dB. Pressure is a field quantity, so doubling it quadruples intensity, which is about +6 dB.

options.text: About 188 dB SPL
options.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic ratios. Doubling the pressure adds a fixed amount; it does not double the decibel number.

options.text: About 100 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. Doubling a pressure ratio adds about 6 dB, so 1 Pa (94 dB SPL) becomes 2 Pa, about 100 dB SPL.

options.text: About 114 dB SPL
options.explanation: +20 dB corresponds to ten times the pressure, not twice.

questions.workedExample:
1. dB SPL compares RMS pressure with a fixed 20 µPa reference using 20 times the logarithm, because pressure is a field quantity.
2. Multiplying the pressure by 2 therefore adds a fixed amount to the level, about 6 dB, whatever the starting level.
3. 94 dB SPL + 6 dB ≈ 100 dB SPL.

The power-quantity rule (3 dB per doubling) applies to intensity or electrical power. Since intensity grows with pressure squared, doubling pressure quadruples intensity, which is 6 dB either way.

lessons.title: Predict free-field distance loss
lessons.summary: Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field.
lessons.body:
## The inverse square law

A small source in open space (a **free field**, with no reflections) spreads its power over the surface of a growing sphere. A sphere's area grows with the square of its radius, so at twice the distance the same acoustic power is shared over four times the area. The **sound intensity** (power per square metre) therefore falls to a quarter, and because intensity is proportional to pressure squared, the RMS pressure halves.

```formula reference
I = P_ac / (4πr^2)
p ∝ 1 / r
where
I: the sound intensity: the acoustic power passing through each square metre, in watts per square metre (W/m²)
P_ac: the acoustic power the source radiates, in watts (W); this is sound power, not the amplifier's electrical power
π: pi, the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159
r: the distance from the source, in metres (m)
p: the RMS sound pressure at distance r, in pascals (Pa)
∝: "is proportional to": when one side is multiplied by some factor, the other is multiplied by the same factor
In words: The same acoustic power is spread over a sphere whose area grows with the square of the distance, so intensity falls with distance squared and pressure falls in proportion to distance.
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a spray can
> Hold a spray can close to a wall and you get a small, dense patch. Step back to twice the distance and the same spray covers a patch twice as wide and twice as tall: four times the area, so each square centimetre gets a quarter of the paint.
>
> **How it maps:** The paint per second is the source's acoustic power, the patch is the sphere the sound spreads over, and paint per square centimetre is intensity. Doubling distance quarters intensity in both cases.
>
> **Where it stops:** Paint droplets fly in straight lines and stick. Sound reflects off walls and bends round objects, so indoors the reflected sound tops the level up and the simple quartering no longer holds.

This is the **inverse square law**. In decibels it becomes a rule about *ratios* of distance, which is what makes it easy to use:

```formula reference
L_2 = L_1 − 20 log_10(r_2 / r_1)
where
L_1: the measured level at distance r_1, in dB SPL
L_2: the predicted level at distance r_2, in dB SPL
r_1: the distance where you know the level, in metres (m)
r_2: the distance you want the level at, in metres (m)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
In words: In decibels the loss depends only on how many times further away you are, not on the extra metres: about 6 dB for every doubling of distance and 20 dB for every tenfold increase.
```

Two landmarks cover almost every estimate:

- Each **doubling of distance** costs about **6 dB**: 1 m to 2 m loses the same as 10 m to 20 m.
- Each **tenfold increase** in distance costs **20 dB**.

So a speaker giving 100 dB SPL at 1 m gives about 94 dB at 2 m, 88 dB at 4 m and 80 dB at 10 m. Counting doublings is usually all you need. The flip side matters for noise problems: walking a few metres further from a source that is already far away barely changes the level, because a few metres is a small *ratio*.

These figures assume the same direction from the source, measurement in its far field (a later lesson explains), negligible air absorption and no reflections. Outdoors, ground reflection, wind and temperature gradients change real results, so treat predictions as first estimates.

> [!warning] Where the law doesn't hold
> - **Indoors**, reflections build a *reverberant field*. Beyond a certain distance (the critical distance) the level stops falling at 6 dB per doubling and levels off. The room-acoustics units cover rooms.
> - **Close to a source**, particularly a large one or a line of speakers, the level doesn't fall in neat inverse-square steps (see the later boundaries and fields unit).
> - **Acoustic line sources** (long columns of speakers) fall closer to 3 dB per doubling over part of their range, because the energy spreads over a cylinder rather than a sphere.

## Key takeaways
- Use the same direction and a source’s free-field far field.
- Each distance doubling reduces pressure level by about six decibels.
- Reflections, line-source geometry and near-field behaviour need different models.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Outdoors, away from reflecting surfaces, a small speaker gives 94 dB SPL at 2 m. Roughly what will you measure at 4 m?

options.text: 47 dB SPL
options.explanation: Doubling distance doesn't halve the decibel value. It subtracts about 6 dB.

options.text: 91 dB SPL
options.explanation: −3 dB per doubling applies to a line source over part of its range, not a small point-like source.

options.text: 94 dB SPL
options.explanation: Sound does lose level with distance in a free field as it spreads over a larger sphere.

options.text: 88 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. Doubling the distance from a point source halves the pressure, which loses about 6 dB.

questions.workedExample:
1. Outdoors, away from reflections, a small source follows the inverse square law in its far field.
2. 2 m to 4 m is one doubling of distance.
3. Each doubling spreads the power over four times the area, halving the pressure, which is about 6 dB.
4. 94 dB − 6 dB ≈ 88 dB SPL.

Note that the answer depends only on the distance ratio: 20 m to 40 m would also lose about 6 dB.

questions.prompt: A PA speaker produces 100 dB SPL at 1 m. Assuming far-field spreading along the same direction, negligible air absorption and free-field conditions, what level reaches a listener 16 m away?

options.text: About 84 dB SPL
options.explanation: This subtracts 16 dB, as if level fell 1 dB per metre. The loss depends on the ratio of distances, not the difference.

options.text: About 76 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. 1 m to 16 m is four doublings (2, 4, 8, 16 m), each costing about 6 dB, so about 24 dB is lost.

options.text: About 88 dB SPL
options.explanation: That is two doublings, which takes you to 4 m. 16 m is four doublings.

options.text: About 94 dB SPL
options.explanation: That is only one doubling, to 2 m.

questions.workedExample:
1. Count doublings from the known distance: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 m is four doublings.
2. In a free field each doubling loses about 6 dB.
3. Four doublings at about 6 dB each is about 24 dB, leaving about 76 dB SPL.

Counting doublings (6 dB each) and tenfold steps (20 dB each) is enough for most estimates. Indoors, reflections would keep the level higher than this.

questions.prompt: At an outdoor event in an open field, the level at a neighbour's boundary 20 m from your speaker is 6 dB over the agreed limit. Assume free-field spreading. Which single change would bring it down by about 6 dB?

options.text: Move the speaker 6 m further back, to 26 m from the boundary
options.explanation: Distance loss depends on the ratio of distances. 26 m is only 1.3 times 20 m, which buys roughly 2 dB, not 6 dB.

options.text: Move the speaker so it is 40 m from the boundary
options.explanation: Correct. Doubling the distance from 20 m to 40 m halves the pressure in a free field, which is about 6 dB.

options.text: Halve the amplifier's output power
options.explanation: Halving power is only about 3 dB. You would need a quarter of the power (half the voltage) for about 6 dB.

options.text: Nothing practical: distance only matters indoors
options.explanation: Distance loss is clearest outdoors in a free field; indoors, reflections make it smaller.

questions.workedExample:
1. In a free field the level depends on the ratio of distances: each doubling costs about 6 dB.
2. 20 m to 40 m is one doubling, so about 6 dB less. 20 m to 26 m is a ratio of only 1.3, which is about 2 dB.
3. Electrically, 6 dB means half the voltage, which is a quarter of the power. Halving the power only gives about 3 dB.

Real outdoor results also depend on ground reflections, wind and temperature, so measure after the change.

lessons.title: Combine unrelated and coherent sources
lessons.summary: Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources.
lessons.body:
## Adding sources

When two sources play at once, how much louder does it get? The answer depends on whether the two waveforms are related.

**Unrelated (incoherent) sources.** Independent sources, such as two air-conditioning units, two singers or a synth and the room's background noise, have waveforms with no fixed relationship. Over a long enough averaging time their peaks sometimes line up and sometimes cancel, and the cross-term averages to zero. What adds is their **mean-square pressure**, which is proportional to power, not their pressures. To combine levels, convert each one back into a relative power, add those powers and convert the total back into decibels:

```formula reference
L_total = 10 log_10(Σ 10^{L_i / 10})
where
L_total: the combined level at the listening position, in dB SPL
L_i: the level of source number i on its own, at the same position, in dB SPL
i: a counter that runs over the sources: 1, 2, 3 and so on
10^{L_i / 10}: the relative power of source i (10 raised to the power of its level divided by 10)
Σ: sigma, "sum of": add up the term for every source
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
In words: Turn each level back into a relative power, add the powers and turn the total back into decibels; decibels themselves never add directly.
```

The useful results:

- Two equal unrelated sources: **+3 dB** (twice the power).
- Four equal unrelated sources: **+6 dB**.
- A source 10 dB quieter than another adds only about **0.4 dB**. The loud one dominates the total, although the quieter one may still be audible if it occupies different frequencies or moments.

**Coherent sources** are different. Two speakers playing the *same* signal add in **pressure**, because their waveforms have a fixed relationship. Where the two arrivals are in phase, the pressure doubles: up to **+6 dB**. Where they arrive half a cycle apart, they cancel deeply.

| Two equal sources | What adds | Best-case change |
|---|---|---|
| Unrelated | power | about +3 dB |
| Identical, in phase | pressure | about +6 dB |
| Identical, half a cycle apart | pressure | deep cancellation |

Whether two copies are in phase depends on the difference in path length compared with the wavelength, so it changes with frequency and listening position. For delayed broadband copies, the repeating frequency peaks and notches are **comb filtering**; a single tone instead shows spatial interference. This is why the microphone lessons' 3:1 rule and the crossover lessons' driver alignment exist.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: pushing a swing
> Two people push a child on a swing. If they push together at exactly the right moment each time, every shove adds and the swing goes much higher. If one pushes forwards while the other pulls back, they cancel out. If they each push at random moments, sometimes helping and sometimes fighting, the swing still gains energy on average, but much less dramatically.
>
> **How it maps:** Pushers in step are coherent, in-phase sources whose pressures add (+6 dB). Pushers fighting each other are coherent sources half a cycle apart, which cancel. Random pushers are unrelated sources: only their average energy adds (+3 dB).
>
> **Where it stops:** A swing has one natural rhythm and one position. Sound covers many frequencies, and the phase relationship between two speakers changes with frequency and with where you stand, so the same pair can reinforce in one seat and cancel in the next.

## Key takeaways
- Uncorrelated sources add in mean-square pressure, giving about three decibels for two equal sources.
- Identical in-phase copies double pressure, giving about six decibels.
- Delayed broadband copies can create comb filtering.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Two unrelated noise sources (say, two air-conditioning units) each produce 85 dB SPL at your position. What is the combined level?

options.text: 170 dB SPL
options.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic; you can't add them arithmetically.

options.text: 91 dB SPL
options.explanation: +6 dB applies to two *coherent* copies of the same signal arriving in phase, not unrelated sources.

options.text: 88 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. Incoherent sources add in power, and doubling the power adds about 3 dB.

options.text: 85 dB SPL
options.explanation: Adding a second source does add energy.

questions.workedExample:
1. Two air-conditioning units are unrelated sources: their waveforms have no fixed relationship.
2. Over time their peaks line up and cancel at random, so on average their powers add, not their pressures.
3. Two equal powers are twice one power, which is +3 dB.
4. 85 dB + 3 dB ≈ 88 dB SPL.

Adding decibel numbers (170 dB) is meaningless, and +6 dB needs identical in-phase copies.

questions.prompt: At the mix position your synth measures 90 dB SPL. The room's background noise (air conditioning) is 80 dB SPL there on its own. You switch the air conditioning off. How much does the meter reading drop?

options.text: About 3 dB
options.explanation: A 3 dB change happens when two equal sources become one. Here the noise has a tenth of the synth's power.

options.text: About 10 dB
options.explanation: The total was never 10 dB above the synth alone. The synth dominated the combined level.

options.text: To about 85 dB SPL
options.explanation: Levels do not average. Removing a quieter source cannot take the total below the louder source on its own.

options.text: By less than half a decibel
options.explanation: Correct. A source 10 dB below another contributes a tenth of the power, raising the total by only about 0.4 dB, so removing it lowers the reading by about that much.

questions.workedExample:
1. The synth and the air conditioning are unrelated, so their powers add.
2. 10 dB less means a tenth of the power. The combined power is 1.1 times the synth's, which is only about 0.4 dB more than the synth alone: about 90.4 dB SPL.
3. Switching the noise off returns the reading to about 90 dB SPL, a drop of about 0.4 dB.

That tiny meter change does not prove the noise was inaudible: masking depends on frequency content, timing and the listener, and the quiet passages of the music may have been exposed to it.

questions.prompt: Which statements about combining two sources at a listener's position are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Two singers each at 80 dB SPL give about 83 dB SPL together
options.explanation: Correct. Independent sources are incoherent, so their powers add: +3 dB.

options.text: Two speakers playing the same signal always add +6 dB everywhere in the room
options.explanation: Equal coherent copies can cancel at positions where their path difference is half a wavelength. For delayed broadband copies this produces comb filtering across frequency; a single tone instead shows spatial interference.

options.text: Coherent sources can partly cancel at some frequencies and positions
options.explanation: Correct. When arrivals are out of phase, pressures subtract.

options.text: Two identical subwoofers fed the same signal, equidistant from you, can give up to +6 dB at low frequencies
options.explanation: Correct. Coherent, in-phase signals add in pressure, and doubling the pressure adds about 6 dB.

questions.workedExample:
1. Ask first whether the two sources are copies of each other.
2. Independent singers are unrelated: their powers add, so two equal ones give about +3 dB.
3. Identical signals are coherent: their pressures add. In phase that is up to +6 dB; half a cycle apart they cancel.
4. Which case applies depends on the path difference compared with the wavelength, so it varies with frequency and position. Two subwoofers equidistant from you are in phase at low frequencies (up to +6 dB), while elsewhere in the room or at higher frequencies the same pair can partly cancel.

lessons.title: Relating wavelength to boundaries and fields
lessons.summary: Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows.
lessons.body:
## Reflection, absorption and diffraction

At a boundary, sound can be reflected, transmitted or absorbed; diffraction describes spreading around edges and openings. Wavelength, impedance and construction all matter.

**Sound reflection.** A hard, large, flat surface (a wall, a desk, a window) reflects sound like a mirror reflects light: angle in equals angle out. This only works well when the surface is large compared with the wavelength. A stiff 30 cm panel can give a directional reflection at 10 kHz (wavelength 3.4 cm). At 100 Hz (wavelength 3.4 m), diffraction around it is important; its actual reflection and transmission still depend on material and mounting.

**Sound absorption.** Porous materials (mineral wool, thick fabric) turn some of the sound's energy into heat. Each material has an **absorption coefficient**: the fraction of the arriving energy that is not returned as reflected sound, in the room-acoustics convention (it may include energy transmitted through the surface). It has no unit and runs from 0, a perfect reflector, to 1, where nothing comes back, as from an open window. A panel that reflects 30 % of the arriving energy has an absorption coefficient of 0.7.

The coefficient varies with frequency, so it is quoted per octave band. Thin foam absorbs high frequencies well and does almost nothing to bass, because bass wavelengths are far longer than the foam is thick.

**Diffraction.** Waves bend around obstacles and spread out through openings. When an obstacle is small compared with the wavelength, sound diffracts around it with hardly a shadow. When it's large, it casts an acoustic shadow. This is why you can hear the bass, but not the cymbals, from a band round the corner; why your head shadows high frequencies but not low ones (the hearing units); and why a loudspeaker radiates almost equally in all directions at low frequencies but beams forward at high frequencies (the loudspeaker-driver units).

| Size vs wavelength | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Object much smaller | Sound diffracts round it |
| Comparable | Partial, frequency-dependent |
| Object much larger | Reflection and shadowing |

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: sea waves at a harbour
> Ocean swell meets a thin mooring post and simply closes up behind it; the water just behind the post is as choppy as anywhere else. The same swell meeting a long harbour wall leaves a calm patch of water in its lee.
>
> **How it maps:** The post is an object much smaller than the wavelength, so the wave diffracts round it with almost no shadow, like bass passing a person or a speaker stand. The harbour wall is much larger than the wavelength, so it reflects and shadows, like a building blocking cymbals.
>
> **Where it stops:** Sea waves move along a surface and are easy to see; sound spreads in three dimensions as pressure. Whether a real surface reflects, transmits or absorbs sound also depends on its material and mounting, which the size comparison alone does not tell you.

## Near field and far field

Very close to a source, the sound field is complicated: different parts of the source (the cone, the edges of the cabinet, several drivers) are at noticeably different distances from you, and their contributions interfere. Level can change sharply as you move a few centimetres, and it doesn't follow the inverse square law.

Further away, in the **far field**, the source behaves like a point: level falls 6 dB per doubling, and the balance between drivers settles down. The distance needed depends on source geometry, frequency and the measurement criterion. Several source dimensions alone is not a universal far-field test for a large array; follow the manufacturer's measurement method and verify that distance-scaled responses converge. Datasheet figures are quoted "at 1 m", but large speakers are often measured further away and the result scaled back to 1 m with the inverse square law.

> [!tip] "Near-field monitor" means something else
> Studio "near-field monitors" are small speakers listened to from about 1–2 m, so that you hear more direct sound than room reflections. They aren't about the acoustic near field of the speaker itself. The room-acoustics units cover them.

## Key takeaways
- Size relative to wavelength affects diffraction and acoustic shadows.
- Absorption also depends on material, mounting and incidence angle.
- A reverberant room and an acoustic near field do not follow a simple distance law.

## Further reading
- [Wave motion — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/waves/wavemotion.html)
- [Sound intensity and decibels — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/intens.html)
- [Speed of sound — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Sound/souspe.html)
- [Inverse square law — HyperPhysics, Georgia State](http://hyperphysics.phy-astr.gsu.edu/hbase/Acoustic/invsqs.html)

questions.prompt: Which of these behaviours depend mainly on the size of an object compared with the wavelength? Select all that apply.

options.text: Thin acoustic foam absorbs high frequencies but barely touches bass
options.explanation: Correct. Porous absorbers need a thickness that's a meaningful fraction of the wavelength to work.

options.text: Sound in air travels faster when it's warm
options.explanation: That depends on temperature, not on object size or wavelength.

options.text: A stiff 30 cm panel can give a directional reflection at 10 kHz, while diffraction around it matters at 100 Hz
options.explanation: Correct as a size comparison. The wavelengths are about 3.4 cm and 3.4 m respectively. Material impedance, thickness, mounting and incidence also determine reflection and transmission.

options.text: You hear the bass but not the cymbals of a band playing round a corner
options.explanation: Correct. Long bass wavelengths diffract round the building; short high-frequency wavelengths are shadowed.

questions.workedExample:
1. Wavelengths in air run from about 3.4 m at 100 Hz to about 34 cm at 1 kHz and 3.4 cm at 10 kHz.
2. Compare each object with the wavelength:
  - A 30 cm panel is about ten times a 10 kHz wavelength, so it can reflect directionally; at 100 Hz it is about a tenth of a wavelength, so sound diffracts round it.
  - A building is far larger than cymbal wavelengths (shadow) but not much larger than bass wavelengths (they bend round it).
  - Thin foam is a tiny fraction of a bass wavelength, so it barely affects bass.
3. Sound being faster in warm air is a temperature effect on speed, not a size effect.

Material, thickness, mounting and incidence angle also decide how much is reflected, transmitted or absorbed.

questions.prompt: Indoors, you measure a speaker at 1, 2, 4 and 8 m: 90, 85, 82 and 81 dB SPL. Why doesn't it lose 6 dB per doubling?

options.text: Reflections build a reverberant field whose level is roughly constant across the room, so beyond some distance it dominates the direct sound
options.explanation: Correct. Close in, the direct sound dominates and falls with distance; further out the reverberant level takes over and the total levels off.

options.text: The meter is faulty; the inverse square law always holds
options.explanation: The law assumes a free field with no reflections. Rooms aren't free fields.

options.text: The speaker is too quiet for the law to apply
options.explanation: The inverse square law doesn't depend on level.

options.text: Sound travels more slowly indoors
options.explanation: The speed of sound depends on air temperature, not on being indoors, and wouldn't change level anyway.

1. Direct sound alone: 90, 84, 78, 72 dB (−6 dB per doubling).
2. Measured: 90, 85, 82, 81 dB, levelling off.
3. The extra is reflected sound. In a room, the reverberant field is roughly uniform, so as the direct sound falls the total approaches the reverberant level.
4. The distance where direct and reverberant levels are equal is called the **critical distance**. The room-acoustics units cover reverberation.

lessons.title: Why equal SPL is not equal loudness
lessons.summary: Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level.
lessons.body:
A sound level meter measures pressure. You hear something else: loudness, pitch, direction and timbre, all built by your ear and brain from that pressure. **Psychoacoustics** studies the gap between the two. For anyone mixing, designing speakers or building instruments it explains why a bass line vanishes at low volume, why a quiet pad disappears under a loud lead, and why a delay speaker can be louder than the stage without pulling the image towards it.

It also explains how hearing gets damaged. That part is not optional reading.

## The range of hearing

The commonly quoted range is **20 Hz to 20 kHz**. Treat both ends as soft:

- The top end falls with age and noise exposure. Many adults hear little above 15–16 kHz. Your synth's 18 kHz content may be inaudible to you and obvious to a teenager (or to your dog).
- At the bottom, below about 20 Hz, very loud sound is felt more than heard.
- Hearing is most sensitive roughly between **2 and 5 kHz**, partly because the ear canal resonates in that region.

In level, hearing spans from the threshold near 0 dB SPL at mid frequencies to very high levels that can cause pain and damage. Pain thresholds vary, and harmful exposure can occur far below pain; a 120 dB level difference represents a millionfold pressure ratio.

## Equal-loudness contours

Play a 100 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone at the same dB SPL and the 100 Hz tone sounds much quieter. An **equal-loudness contour** joins up the levels at which pure tones of different frequencies sound equally loud. Each contour is labelled in **phons**: for example, the forty-phon contour passes through 40 dB SPL at one kilohertz. The standard specifies young, otologically normal listeners, frontal free-field pure tones and binaural listening; it is not a calibration of every listener or broadband music.

The first such curves were Fletcher and Munson's (1933). The current international standard is **ISO 226**. Its 2003 edition replaced older curves that had been shown to be inaccurate, and it was revised again in **2023** with small changes.

```diagram
 dB SPL
 120 |\                        /
     | \___  80 phon     ___/
  80 |     \___________/
     |\
  40 | \___  20 phon     __/
     |     \___________/
   0 +-----+-----+-----+-----+
     20   100    1k    5k   20k Hz
```

(A sketch of the shape only: read real values and listening conditions from the applicable ISO 226 edition.)

Three things to take from the curves:

- **Bass needs much more SPL** than mid frequencies to sound equally loud, especially at low listening levels.
- **The curves flatten as level rises.** The difference between bass and mids is smaller at 80 phon than at 20 phon.
- So **a mix sounds different at different volumes.** Turn it down and the bass and extreme treble seem to fade first. Mix at one consistent, moderate level, and check at quiet and loud levels.

## Key takeaways
- Hearing sensitivity varies with frequency, listener and sound level.
- Equal-loudness contours describe pure tones under specified conditions.
- A mix’s perceived balance changes with listening level.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)
- [ISO 226:2023 scope and history — Estonian standards body](https://www.evs.ee/en/iso-226-2023)

questions.prompt: You play a 60 Hz tone and a 1 kHz tone, both at 50 dB SPL. How do they compare in loudness?

options.text: The 60 Hz tone sounds much quieter
options.explanation: Correct. The equal-loudness contours show low frequencies need considerably more SPL to sound as loud as 1 kHz at moderate levels.

options.text: They sound equally loud because the SPL is the same
options.explanation: Equal SPL doesn't mean equal loudness. Hearing is much less sensitive at low frequencies, especially at low levels.

options.text: The 60 Hz tone sounds much louder
options.explanation: It's the reverse: hearing is least sensitive at the low end.

options.text: You can't hear 60 Hz at all
options.explanation: 60 Hz is inside the audible range, just at reduced sensitivity.

questions.workedExample:
1. Equal-loudness contours (ISO 226) show the SPL needed at each frequency to match the loudness of a 1 kHz tone.
2. At low phon levels the contours rise steeply below a few hundred hertz.
3. So at 50 dB SPL, the 60 Hz tone is well below the loudness of the 1 kHz tone.
4. Practical consequence: turning a mix down makes the bass seem to disappear first.

options.explanation: Loudspeakers are broadly linear; their frequency response doesn't change that much with level.

lessons.title: Understand A, C and Z weighting
lessons.summary: A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading.
lessons.body:
## A and C weighting

Sound level meters apply a **frequency weighting** to make a single number track human response better. The two that matter, both defined for sound level meters in **IEC 61672-1**:

- **A-weighting** (dB(A) or dBA) strongly reduces low frequencies (about −19 dB at 100 Hz, −30 dB at 50 Hz) and slightly boosts 2–4 kHz. It was based on the 40-phon Fletcher–Munson curve. It is the standard weighting for noise exposure and for many noise-floor specifications.
- **C-weighting** (dB(C)) is nearly flat from about 31.5 Hz to 8 kHz (−3 dB points). It is used for **peak level** measurements, and for loud, bass-heavy sound where A-weighting would hide the low end.
- **Z-weighting** is flat ("zero").

In Great Britain, the Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005 express daily or weekly exposure in dB(A) and peak sound pressure in dB(C) (the next lessons cover the limits).

Because a weighting removes part of the spectrum before the meter measures, the same sound gives different readings under different weightings. Approximate A-weighting values, from the IEC 61672-1 definition:

| Frequency | A-weighting |
|---|---|
| 31.5 Hz | about −39 dB |
| 50 Hz | about −30 dB |
| 100 Hz | about −19 dB |
| 1 kHz | 0 dB |
| 2–4 kHz | about +1 dB |
| 10 kHz | about −2.5 dB |

So a 100 Hz tone read on an A-weighted meter shows about 19 dB less than its unweighted sound pressure level. A dB(A) figure is therefore a statement about a *filtered* measurement, and two sounds with the same dB(A) can have very different amounts of bass.

The curve is not a vague idea: IEC 61672-1 defines it exactly, as a fixed combination of simple filters. You do not need the formula to read meters, but it is the starting point if you build an A-weighted meter in software:

```formula reference
R_A = 12194^2 f^4 / D
D = (f^2 + 20.6^2)(f^2 + 12194^2)
  √((f^2 + 107.7^2)(f^2 + 737.9^2))
A = 20 log_10(R_A) + 2.00
where
R_A: the A-weighting response at frequency f, as a plain gain ratio (no unit)
f: the frequency being weighted, in hertz (Hz)
D: the denominator, written on its own lines only to keep them short
20.6, 107.7, 737.9, 12194: the corner frequencies of the weighting's filter stages, in hertz (Hz)
√: square root
log_10: the base-10 logarithm: the power you raise 10 to in order to get the number
2.00: a rounded correction in decibels that makes the weighting approximately 0 dB at 1 kHz
A: the A-weighting at frequency f, in decibels (dB); negative means the meter reduces that frequency
In words: A-weighting is a fixed filter defined in the standard: two stages cut below about 20 Hz, stages near 108 Hz and 738 Hz shape the low-mid roll-off, two stages cut above about 12 kHz, and an offset sets 1 kHz to 0 dB.
```

> [!note] Why live engineers watch dB(C) as well as dB(A)
> A kick drum and sub-bass can carry enormous energy at 40–60 Hz while barely moving a dB(A) meter. Venues often monitor both.

## Key takeaways
- A-weighting strongly attenuates low-frequency contributions to a meter reading.
- Great Britain workplace exposure uses A-weighting for dose and C-weighting for peaks.
- Weightings are measurement filters, not a loudspeaker behaviour.

## Further reading
- [A-weighting measurement implementation — Son, Kyung and Cho (2019)](https://mdpi-res.com/d_attachment/sensors/sensors-19-03633/article_deploy/sensors-19-03633.pdf)
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

options.text: C for exposure, A for peaks
options.explanation: It's the other way round.

options.explanation: Exposure regulations use A-weighting for the daily dose and C-weighting for peaks.

options.explanation: A-weighting would understate the low-frequency content of impulsive peaks; C-weighting is used for those.

lessons.title: Masking and auditory filter bandwidth
lessons.summary: Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level.
lessons.body:
## Masking

A loud sound can make a quieter one inaudible. This is **masking**, and it's the reason a mix "gets muddy": parts that each sound fine alone hide each other when played together.

- **Simultaneous masking** is strongest when the two sounds are **close in frequency**.
- It **spreads upwards**: a loud low sound masks higher frequencies much more effectively than a loud high sound masks lower ones. The effect grows with level. That's why a heavy bass part can dull a whole mix.
- **Temporal masking** also happens: a loud sound can hide quieter sounds just after it (and, briefly, just before it).

Lossy codecs such as MP3 and AAC exploit masking: they spend fewer bits on what masking will hide anyway.

## Critical bands, intuitively

The cochlea behaves like a bank of overlapping band-pass filters. Critical-band measurements and auditory-filter bandwidths both describe frequency selectivity, but their numerical widths depend on how they are measured. ERB is the width of an ideal rectangular filter with the same peak gain and integrated response as the actual filter. Two tones inside one band interact strongly: they mask each other, beat or sound rough. Tones in well-separated bands are heard more independently.

The bands are narrow at low frequencies and wider at high frequencies. One standard model, Glasberg and Moore's **equivalent rectangular bandwidth (ERB)**, gives the width of the auditory filter centred on a given frequency. It was fitted to listening-test data from young, normally hearing listeners at moderate levels. In words: the auditory filter is about 25 Hz wide at the very bottom of the range and widens roughly in proportion to frequency, approaching about 11 % of the centre frequency at high frequencies.

| Centre | ERB |
|---|---|
| 100 Hz | ≈ 35 Hz |
| 1 kHz | ≈ 133 Hz |
| 4 kHz | ≈ 456 Hz |

```formula reference
ERB = 24.7 (4.37f / 1000 + 1)
where
ERB: the equivalent rectangular bandwidth of the auditory filter, in hertz (Hz)
f: the centre frequency of the filter, in hertz (Hz)
24.7: the bandwidth in hertz the formula gives at very low frequencies
4.37: how fast the bandwidth grows with frequency, per kilohertz of centre frequency
1000: converts f from hertz to kilohertz
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: Glasberg and Moore's fit gives an auditory filter about 25 Hz wide at very low frequencies, widening in proportion to frequency towards about 11 % of the centre frequency.
```

The formula is an average fit, not a sharp boundary: real filters overlap, and their widths change with level and between listeners.

The practical consequence is that a fixed spacing in hertz means very different things in different registers. Two bass parts a few tens of hertz apart fall inside the same or neighbouring auditory filters, while two bright parts the same number of hertz apart at 4 kHz are, to the ear, practically on top of each other. EQ-ing space between parts, or choosing different octaves, does more for clarity than turning one of them up.

## Key takeaways
- Masking depends on spectrum, timing and level.
- Auditory filters overlap and generally widen as centre frequency rises.
- ERB summarizes a filter response; it is not a sharp separation boundary.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)

- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

options.text: The precedence effect
options.explanation: That concerns localisation of first-arriving sounds, not one sound hiding another in frequency.

options.text: Interaural level difference
options.explanation: That's a localisation cue, not a masking effect.

options.text: The upward spread of masking
options.explanation: Correct. Masking spreads more towards frequencies above the masker, and the spread grows with level.

options.text: A-weighting
options.explanation: A weighting is a meter filter, not a perceptual effect.

questions.workedExample:
1. Masking is strongest within a critical band around the masker.
2. The masking pattern is asymmetric: it extends much further upward than downward, especially at high levels.
3. So a loud low sound can mask higher sounds, but a loud high sound does little to lower ones.
4. Fix in a mix: reduce the bass level or carve its upper harmonics with EQ.

questions.prompt: Glasberg and Moore's model gives an auditory filter (ERB) about 35 Hz wide at 100 Hz and about 456 Hz wide at 4 kHz. Two pairs of tones are each 60 Hz apart: one pair near 100 Hz, the other near 4 kHz. Which pair is more likely to interact strongly (masking, beating or roughness)?

options.text: The pair near 4 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. 60 Hz is a small fraction of a roughly 456 Hz auditory filter, so both tones fall in essentially the same band. Near 100 Hz, 60 Hz is nearly two filter widths, so the tones are resolved more independently.

options.text: The pair near 100 Hz, because bass always masks more
options.explanation: Upward spread of masking concerns a loud low sound masking higher ones. Here the question is how close each pair is relative to its own auditory filter width.

options.text: Both equally, because they are the same number of hertz apart
options.explanation: Auditory filters widen with frequency, so the same spacing in hertz is close in one register and far apart in another.

options.text: Neither, because 60 Hz is always outside one auditory filter
options.explanation: At 4 kHz the filter is several hundred hertz wide, so 60 Hz is well inside it.

questions.workedExample:
1. Compare each spacing with the auditory filter width at that frequency, not with a fixed number of hertz.
2. Near 100 Hz: the filter is about 35 Hz wide, so 60 Hz apart is close to two filter widths. The tones excite largely different filters.
3. Near 4 kHz: the filter is about 456 Hz wide, so 60 Hz apart is about an eighth of a width. Both tones fall in the same filter and interact strongly.
4. The ERB is an average fit with overlapping filters, so this is a tendency rather than a sharp boundary; level, timing and the listener also matter.

Mixing consequence: separate parts by register, or by a meaningful fraction of the local band, rather than by a fixed number of hertz.

lessons.title: Locate sound and understand precedence
lessons.summary: Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies.
lessons.body:
## Localisation: ITD and ILD

You locate a sound left or right mainly from two cues:

- **Interaural time difference (ITD).** A sound from the side reaches the near ear first. Maximum adult ITDs are of order 0.6–0.7 ms and vary with head size, frequency and source direction; simply dividing ear spacing by sound speed neglects diffraction around the head. ITD (as phase differences) is the main cue at **low frequencies**, below about 1 kHz.
- **Interaural level difference (ILD).** The head casts an acoustic shadow, but only for wavelengths small compared with the head (the acoustics units’ diffraction rule). So ILD is the main cue at **high frequencies**, above about 1.5 kHz.

Between roughly 1 and 1.5 kHz both cues contribute. This "duplex theory" goes back to Lord Rayleigh (1907). Neither cue separates front from back or up from down; for those the brain uses the filtering of the **outer ear (pinna)** and small head movements.

> [!tip] Why one subwoofer is usually enough
> At very low frequencies the head casts almost no shadow (so ILD vanishes), the interaural time difference becomes a tiny fraction of a cycle, and in a room the modes and reflections swamp what cues remain. So localisation of deep bass is poor, which is why a single subwoofer can usually be placed off-centre without the bass seeming to come from it. An 80 Hz crossover is a common system choice, not a hard hearing boundary; it only works if the crossover is low and the sub's distortion and port noise don't add higher-frequency content you *can* locate.

## The precedence (Haas) effect

In a room, you hear the direct sound plus many reflections from other directions, yet you perceive one sound coming from the source. The **precedence effect** is the reason: the auditory system localises a sound by the **first-arriving wavefront** and suppresses the direction of early reflections.

Precedence depends on signal, level, delay, direction and listening conditions. Fusion (hearing one event), localization dominance (hearing it toward the first source), and suppression of information about the reflection are related but distinct; one can persist after another breaks down. There is no universal delay/level boundary guaranteeing all three. Exact Haas-derived limits are absent here because their original experimental conditions were not reliably established in this review.

This has a direct engineering use (the sound-system lessons): a **delay speaker** halfway down a field is held back electronically so that its sound arrives *with or just after* the sound from the stage. If it played undelayed, listeners near it would hear it first, localise the band to the delay tower, and then hear the stage arriving later as an echo.

The starting setting is the difference between the stage-to-listener and fill-to-listener travel times (sound covers about 34.3 m in 100 ms), plus any small precedence offset you deliberately choose so the stage wins the race:

```formula reference
t_delay = (d_main − d_fill) / c + t_off
where
t_delay: the electronic delay applied to the delay speaker, in seconds (s) or milliseconds (ms)
d_main: the distance from the main stage speakers to the listener, in metres (m)
d_fill: the distance from the delay speaker to the listener, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
t_off: an extra delay, expressed in the same time unit as the path-time term, chosen so the stage sound arrives first; an example to evaluate by listening, not a fixed rule
In words: Hold back the delay speaker by the extra time the stage sound needs to reach the listener, plus a little more if you choose, so the stage wins the race.
```

This starting point ignores electronic latency and temperature changes. Account for the latency of the processing in each path, then measure and listen across the coverage area. A large offset can cause audible echoes or comb filtering rather than guarantee stage localisation.

## Key takeaways
- Time differences dominate low-frequency left–right localisation; level differences matter strongly at high frequencies.
- Outer-ear filtering and head movements provide additional direction cues.
- Delay alignment uses path and electronic-latency differences; an extra offset is a design choice to evaluate.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: Which statements about left–right localisation are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: ILD is large at 100 Hz because the head blocks the sound
options.explanation: At 100 Hz the wavelength (3.4 m) is far larger than the head, so sound diffracts round it and ILD is tiny.

options.text: Maximum adult ITDs are of order 0.6–0.7 ms
options.explanation: Correct as an approximate scale; head geometry, diffraction and frequency affect the value.

options.text: ITD is the main cue at low frequencies, below about 1 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. Long wavelengths make phase differences between the ears unambiguous.

options.text: ILD is the main cue at high frequencies, above about 1.5 kHz
options.explanation: Correct. The head only shadows wavelengths that are small compared with it.

questions.workedExample:
- ITD: time (phase) difference. Max is of order 0.6–0.7 ms; ear-spacing divided by sound speed is only a crude illustration. Unambiguous when the half-wavelength is larger than the head, i.e. at low frequencies.
- ILD: level difference from head shadowing. Needs wavelengths comparable with or smaller than the head, i.e. high frequencies.
- Between about 1 and 1.5 kHz both contribute (Rayleigh's duplex theory).

questions.prompt: A delay speaker stands partway down a field and is fed with no delay. Listeners near it say the band seems to come from the delay tower, followed by a slap echo from the stage. The stage sound takes about 100 ms longer to reach them than the delay speaker's sound. What is the best starting fix?

options.text: Turn the delay speaker up so it covers the echo
options.explanation: Making it louder strengthens the early arrival from the tower, so the image stays on the tower and the late stage arrival remains a separate echo.

options.text: Delay it by about 100 ms plus a small chosen offset, then measure and listen
options.explanation: Correct. Matching the extra stage travel time, with a little more so the stage arrives first, lets precedence pull the image towards the stage and removes the echo. Latency and conditions mean the setting must be checked on site.

options.text: Delay it by only 10–20 ms
options.explanation: That is just the optional offset. The tower would still arrive about 80–90 ms before the stage sound.

options.text: Delay it by about one second
options.explanation: Far too long: the tower would now arrive long after the stage, as a separate echo of its own.

questions.workedExample:
1. Precedence: listeners localise towards the first-arriving wavefront.
2. Undelayed, the nearby tower arrives about 100 ms before the stage. The image moves to the tower, and the stage sound arrives so much later that it is heard as an echo.
3. Delaying the tower by the travel-time difference (about 100 ms) lines the two arrivals up; a small deliberate offset lets the stage arrive first.
4. The offset is a design choice, not a universal rule. Account for processing latency and temperature, then check localisation, intelligibility and echoes across the coverage area.

lessons.title: Great Britain workplace noise duties
lessons.summary: Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time.
lessons.body:
## Hearing damage and safe exposure

Noise-induced hearing loss is permanent. It depends on **level and time together**: the dose. Tinnitus (ringing) after a loud session is a warning sign.

**Great Britain workplaces: Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005** (HSE). These apply to music and entertainment work too.

| Threshold | Daily LEP,d / weekly LEP,w | Peak (LCpeak) |
|---|---|---|
| Lower action value | 80 dB(A) | 135 dB(C) |
| Upper action value | 85 dB(A) | 137 dB(C) |
| Exposure limit | 87 dB(A) | 140 dB(C) |

At the lower action value the employer must assess the risk, provide information and training, and make hearing protection available to anyone who asks for it; at the upper one, hearing protection and hearing protection zones become mandatory. The exposure limit values take account of the reduction given by hearing protection and must not be exceeded; the action values do not (regulation 4(5)), so they're judged on unprotected exposure.

## Key takeaways
- Workplace noise risk depends on level and exposure time.
- Action values use unprotected exposure.
- The exposure limit takes hearing protection into account; peak exposure also needs assessment.

## Further reading
- [Auditory processing — Brian C. J. Moore](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2606789/)
- [Noise regulations — HSE](https://www.hse.gov.uk/noise/regulations.htm)
- [Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005, regulation 4](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/uksi/2005/1643/regulation/4/made)
- [WHO safe-listening venues standard summary](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/mls_whd_infographic.pdf?sfvrsn=93a7a1ef_5)

options.explanation: Correct. The upper exposure action value is 85 dB(A) (and a peak of 137 dB(C)).
That is the WHO venue recommendation (LAeq over 15 minutes), not a UK workplace action value.

lessons.title: Noise dose and safe-listening guidance
lessons.summary: NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate.
lessons.body:
## Noise dose and listening guidance

**NIOSH (US) recommended exposure limit:** **85 dB(A)** averaged over an eight-hour day, with a **3 dB noise-dose exchange rate**: every 3 dB increase halves the allowed time. A 3 dB increase doubles the sound energy, so halving the time keeps the total energy (the dose) the same.

| Steady level | Time to reach the NIOSH reference dose |
|---|---|
| 85 dB(A) | 8 hours |
| 88 dB(A) | 4 hours |
| 91 dB(A) | 2 hours |
| 94 dB(A) | 1 hour |
| 97 dB(A) | 30 minutes |
| 100 dB(A) | 15 minutes |

```formula reference
T = 480 / 2^{(L − 85) / 3}
where
T: the time to reach the NIOSH reference daily dose, in minutes (min)
480: eight hours, in minutes
L: the steady A-weighted exposure level, in dB(A)
85: the NIOSH recommended exposure limit for eight hours, in dB(A)
3: the noise-dose exchange rate, in decibels: each 3 dB step halves the time
2^{(L − 85) / 3}: 2 raised to the number of 3 dB steps above 85 dB(A)
In words: Start from eight hours at 85 dB(A) and halve the time for every 3 dB louder.
```

So a steady 100 dB(A), a level easily reached near a PA or in loud headphones, reaches the NIOSH reference daily dose in **15 minutes**, before adding any other exposure that day. Exposures add up: an hour at 94 dB(A) in the afternoon and another at a gig in the evening make two full doses. This is a risk-management limit, not a guarantee of no hearing damage.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a daily spending allowance
> Imagine a fixed daily allowance. At one shop you can browse all day before it runs out; at a pricier shop, where everything costs twice as much, it lasts half as long, and every visit anywhere that day comes out of the same allowance.
>
> **How it maps:** The allowance is the reference daily noise dose. Each 3 dB louder is a shop with double the prices: the same dose is used up in half the time. Time spent at several loud places adds up against one total.
>
> **Where it stops:** A spending allowance is a hard rule that guarantees nothing bad happens below it. A noise dose is a population risk guideline: staying under it does not guarantee no damage for every person, and the ear does not simply reset at midnight.

**WHO:**
- The WHO–ITU standard for personal audio devices sets a reference weekly allowance of **80 dB for 40 hours a week** for adults (75 dB for children).
- The **WHO Global Standard for Safe Listening Venues and Events** (2022) recommends a maximum of **100 dB LAeq over any 15 minutes** for audiences, alongside monitoring, hearing protection, quiet zones and other measures. This is a ceiling, not a recommended operating target or a guarantee of safety for an entire event.

> [!warning] Protect your hearing while building and testing
> - Bring levels up gradually. A DIY synth can produce a full-scale square wave or a feedback screech the moment you change a line of code.
> - Set headphone and monitor volume *before* putting headphones on, and start low.
> - Use a limiter on the monitoring path while developing.
> - Wear musicians' earplugs at gigs and loud rehearsals; they reduce level fairly evenly across frequency.

## Key takeaways
- NIOSH’s recommended eight-hour reference is 85 dBA with a three-decibel noise-dose exchange rate.
- Other daily exposures add to the total dose.
- WHO venue and personal-device recommendations use different reference periods and additional protective measures.

## Further reading

- [Noise exposure and exchange rate — NIOSH](https://www.cdc.gov/niosh/noise/about/noise.html)
- [Personal-device reference sound allowances — WHO](https://www.who.int/news-room/questions-and-answers/item/deafness-and-hearing-loss-safe-listening)
- [WHO–ITU personal-device reference allowances](https://cdn.who.int/media/docs/default-source/documents/health-topics/deafness-and-hearing-loss/standard-summary-make-listening-safe.pdf?sfvrsn=fc114686_14)

options.text: 30 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. 97 dBA is 12 dB, or four 3 dB steps, above 85 dBA, so the 8 hours halves four times, to 30 minutes.

2. 97 dBA is 12 dB above 85, which is four 3 dB steps.

Other exposure that day adds to the dose, and staying below it does not guarantee no hearing harm.

lessons.title: How microphone types produce voltage
lessons.summary: Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction.
lessons.body:
A moving-coil microphone resembles a moving-coil loudspeaker run backwards: a light diaphragm moved by sound pressure, connected to something that turns motion into voltage. The way it makes that conversion decides its sensitivity, noise, ruggedness and whether it needs power. The way sound reaches the diaphragm decides its directional pattern.

Even if you mostly record your synth by plugging it straight in (the sound-system units’ DI box), you'll mic amplifiers, voices and rooms, and you'll need to read microphone specifications.

## Three ways to make a voltage

### Dynamic (moving coil)

A small coil of wire is glued to the diaphragm and sits in the gap of a permanent magnet. Sound moves the diaphragm, the coil moves through the magnetic field, and **electromagnetic induction** generates a voltage proportional to its velocity.

- A traditional passive moving-coil mic needs no power; models with internal active electronics are exceptions.
- Rugged and tolerant of very high SPL (kick drums, guitar cabs, vocals on stage).
- The coil adds mass, so transient and high-frequency detail are usually less than a condenser's.
- Low output: typically around 1–3 mV per pascal. Needs plenty of preamp gain.

The Shure SM58 is the classic example.

### Condenser (capacitor)

The diaphragm is one plate of a **capacitor**; a fixed **backplate** is the other. Sound changes the gap, so the capacitance changes. A conventional capsule with an external polarising supply is charged through a very large resistance, so charge is approximately constant over the relevant audio timescale. An **electret** supplies a persistent electric polarisation. Changing capacitance then changes the capsule voltage; the readout electronics and capsule design still matter.

- The capsule has an extremely high impedance, so a conventional studio condenser microphone uses an **impedance converter** (a small amplifier). That needs power: usually phantom power, sometimes a battery or a dedicated supply for valve models.
- The diaphragm is very light, so condensers capture fast transients and high-frequency detail.
- Often higher output (for example 10–30 mV/Pa). A low-noise condenser can give a quieter recording of a quiet source, but compare the actual microphone and preamp specifications; the operating principle alone does not guarantee lower noise or lower maximum SPL.

### Ribbon

A very thin corrugated metal ribbon hangs in a magnetic field. Sound moves the ribbon, and induction generates a voltage, as in a dynamic mic. The ribbon has a tiny output and very low impedance, so passive ribbons use a step-up transformer.

- Open at front and back, a ribbon naturally has a **figure-8** pattern.
- Smooth, often darker high end.
- Physically fragile: a blast of air (wind, a kick drum port, blowing into it) can stretch the ribbon.

> [!warning] Ribbons and phantom power
> A correctly wired balanced cable puts phantom voltage equally on both signal pins, so an ideal floating passive output sees no differential DC. Damage can still happen with a faulty or miswired cable, with unbalanced adapters, or when hot-plugging with phantom on, because the pins don't make contact at the same instant. Switch phantom power **off** before connecting a passive ribbon (or anything that doesn't need it). Some modern "active" ribbons need phantom: follow the manufacturer's manual.

## Proximity effect

Directional (pressure-gradient) mics have a **bass boost when the source is very close**, within a few centimetres to tens of centimetres. Close to a small source, the pressure difference between the front and back of the diaphragm contains an extra component that is relatively strongest at low frequencies. The closer the source, the bigger the boost.

- Singers use it ("eating the mic" for a warm, big voice).
- It causes boomy, muddy recordings when you didn't want it.
- **Omnidirectional (pure pressure) mics have no proximity effect.**
- Many directional mics have a bass-cut switch to compensate.

## Key takeaways
- Moving-coil and ribbon microphones generate voltage by electromagnetic induction.
- Condenser microphones need power for their impedance-converting electronics.
- Pressure-gradient microphones can show proximity bass boost; pure pressure microphones do not.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
