lessons.title: Read microphone patterns and their nulls
lessons.summary: Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses.
lessons.body:
## Polar patterns

How a mic responds to sound from different directions depends on how the diaphragm is exposed:

- **Pressure microphones** (diaphragm open only at the front, sealed behind) respond to pressure itself, which has no direction: **omnidirectional**.
- **Pressure-gradient** mics (open at front and back) respond to the *difference* in pressure between the two sides. Sound from the side reaches both sides equally, giving a null: **figure-8**.
- Combining the two (or using an acoustic delay network behind the diaphragm) gives the **cardioid family**.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a barometer and a swinging door
> A barometer reports the air pressure in the room; it neither knows nor cares which way the wind blows. A light swinging door, open on both sides, only moves when the push on one face differs from the push on the other: a draught straight through swings it, while a draught sliding past along its face leaves it still.
>
> **How it maps:** The barometer is a pressure (omnidirectional) microphone. The door is a pressure-gradient diaphragm, open front and back: sound from the front or back pushes it, while sound from the side pushes both faces equally and produces the figure-8's side null. Mixing the two behaviours gives the cardioid family.
>
> **Where it stops:** A door responds to steady wind; a diaphragm responds to tiny, rapid pressure changes, and the size of the front-to-back difference depends on frequency and distance. Real cardioids often build the mix with an acoustic delay path behind one diaphragm rather than two separate parts.

All the common ("first-order") patterns are a mix of an omni part, which is the same in every direction, and a figure-8 part, which follows the cosine of the angle. One relationship covers the whole family; only the mix changes:

```formula essential
r(θ) = A + (1 − A) cos(θ)
where
r(θ): the microphone's relative sensitivity to sound arriving from angle θ, as a fraction of its on-axis sensitivity; 1 means as sensitive as straight ahead, 0 means a null (no pickup), and a negative value means a lobe that picks up with inverted polarity
r: the relative sensitivity (see r(θ))
θ: theta, the angle between the sound's direction and the front axis of the mic, in degrees (°); 0° is straight ahead, 90° is the side, 180° is directly behind
A: the omni share of the mix, a pure number from 0 to 1; A = 1 is omni, A = 0 is figure-8, A = 0.5 is cardioid, about 0.37 is supercardioid and 0.25 is hypercardioid
cos: cosine, a function that is 1 at 0°, 0 at 90° and −1 at 180°
In words: the pickup in any direction is the fixed omni part plus the figure-8 part scaled by the cosine of the angle. Lowering A narrows the front but grows a rear lobe.
```

Read it at three landmark angles:

- **At the side (90°)** the cosine is zero, so only the omni share remains. A cardioid (half omni) keeps half its voltage there: about −6 dB.
- **Directly behind (180°)** the figure-8 part is fully negative. For a cardioid it exactly cancels the omni half, giving the rear null. With less omni (super- and hypercardioid), the figure-8 part wins, leaving a **rear lobe** of inverted polarity: a hypercardioid is only about 6 dB down directly behind.
- **The null** sits wherever the figure-8 part exactly cancels the omni part. Less omni moves it forward from 180°: about 125° for a supercardioid, about 110° for a hypercardioid and 90° for a figure-8.

```formula reference
θ_null = arccos(−A / (1 − A))
where
θ_null: the angle at which the ideal pattern picks up nothing, in degrees (°), measured from the front axis
A: the omni share of the mix, a pure number; the expression applies only for A at most 0.5, since patterns with more omni have no null
arccos: the inverse cosine: the angle whose cosine is the given number
In words: For an ideal first-order microphone the null sits where the figure-8 part exactly cancels the omni part; with less omni in the mix, the null swings forward from directly behind towards the sides.
```

| Pattern | Side (90°) | Null |
|---|---|---|
| Omni | 0 dB | none |
| Cardioid | −6 dB | 180° (rear) |
| Supercardioid | ≈ −8.7 dB | ≈ 125° |
| Hypercardioid | −12 dB | ≈ 110° |
| Figure-8 | null | 90° |

Supercardioid definitions vary a little between sources; the table uses an omni share of 0.366, one common choice. An ideal null is complete silence; a real microphone has finite rejection there.

Super- and hypercardioids are narrower at the front but have a **rear lobe** (a hypercardioid is only −6 dB directly behind). That matters for stage monitors (the sound-system units): put a wedge at a cardioid's 180° null, but at the 110–125° nulls of a hyper- or supercardioid.

Real microphones only follow these shapes approximately. Their directionality can change substantially with frequency; a pressure-gradient design can retain low-frequency directionality, while a pressure microphone becomes more directional at high frequencies as its size matters. Check the polar plots in the datasheet.

## Key takeaways
- Ideal first-order patterns combine omnidirectional and figure-eight responses.
- A cardioid’s rear null differs from the angled nulls of hypercardioid and supercardioid patterns.
- Measured polar plots vary with frequency and determine practical placement.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)

questions.prompt: A cardioid microphone points at a singer. From which direction does it reject sound most strongly?

options.text: From the sides (90°)
options.explanation: At 90° the figure-8 part of a cardioid is zero, so the omni half remains: about 6 dB down, not a null.

options.text: From in front (0°)
options.explanation: That is the direction of maximum sensitivity, where the omni and figure-8 parts add.

options.text: From directly behind (180°)
options.explanation: Correct. Directly behind, the figure-8 half is fully negative and exactly cancels the omni half, giving the null.

options.text: Equally from all directions
options.explanation: That describes an omnidirectional mic, which rejects nothing.

questions.workedExample:
1. A cardioid is an equal mix of an omni part (the same everywhere) and a figure-8 part (positive in front, zero at the sides, negative behind).
2. In front both parts add: full sensitivity.
3. At the side the figure-8 part is zero, leaving half: about −6 dB.
4. Directly behind the figure-8 part is fully negative and cancels the omni half: the null.

So a floor monitor goes directly behind a cardioid, as Shure's SM58 guide recommends. Real polar plots vary with frequency, so check them.

questions.prompt: A singer uses a hypercardioid vocal mic on stage. Where should the floor wedge go to get the most gain before feedback?

options.text: Directly behind the mic (180°)
options.explanation: A hypercardioid has a rear lobe: it is only about 6 dB down directly behind, so a wedge there is picked up well.

options.text: At about 110° off-axis, roughly in line with the null
options.explanation: Correct. A hypercardioid's ideal nulls are at about 110°, so a wedge near that angle is picked up least.

options.text: At 90°, directly to the side
options.explanation: At 90° a hypercardioid is about 12 dB down, but its null is further round.

options.text: In front of the mic, facing the singer
options.explanation: That points the wedge into the mic's most sensitive direction.

questions.workedExample:
1. A hypercardioid has only a quarter omni share; the rest is figure-8.
2. Directly behind, the larger figure-8 part outweighs the omni part, leaving a rear lobe about 6 dB down (with inverted polarity).
3. The null is where the two parts cancel exactly. With so little omni share, that happens before 180°: at about 110°.
4. So a wedge at about 110° off-axis, or a pair either side near those angles, is picked up least.

Real patterns vary with frequency: check the datasheet polar plot and test before the show.

lessons.title: Microphone sensitivity, noise and overload
lessons.summary: Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal.
lessons.body:
## Reading the specifications

### Sensitivity

The output voltage for a given sound pressure, normally at 1 kHz and **1 Pa (94 dB SPL)**:

- **mV/Pa**: millivolts of output per pascal of sound pressure, or
- **dBV/Pa**: the same figure in decibels relative to 1 volt per pascal.

Both describe the same thing. dBV/Pa is a voltage ratio in decibels, so every factor of 10 in mV/Pa is 20 dB, and a less negative dBV/Pa figure means more output.

```formula reference
S_dBV = 20 log_10(S / (1 V/Pa))
where
S_dBV: the sensitivity in decibels relative to 1 volt per pascal (dBV/Pa); negative for typical passive and studio microphones, and less negative means more output
S: the sensitivity as a voltage ratio, in volts per pascal (V/Pa); for example 28 mV/Pa = 0.028 V/Pa
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
V: volt, the unit of voltage
Pa: pascal, the unit of pressure; 1 Pa is about 94 dB SPL
dBV: decibels relative to 1 volt
In words: dBV/Pa expresses a microphone's output per pascal as a voltage ratio against one volt per pascal, so 28 millivolts per pascal is about −31 dBV/Pa and 1.6 millivolts per pascal is about −56 dBV/Pa.
```

| Mic (manufacturer's figures) | mV/Pa | dBV/Pa |
|---|---|---|
| Shure SM58 (dynamic) | 1.6 | −56.0 |
| Neumann U 87 Ai, cardioid | 28 | ≈ −31 |

(The SM58 figures follow Shure’s user guide version 6.4 (2024-F), checked October 2026; the −56.0 dBV/Pa figure corresponds to about 1.585 mV/Pa, rounded to 1.6 mV/Pa. The U 87 Ai figures are Neumann's published technical data. Older specifications quote different values, so confirm the revision for the microphone being used.)

The condenser puts out about 17.5 times the voltage of the dynamic, which is about **25 dB**. So for the same recorded level, the dynamic needs about 25 dB more preamp gain. That gain raises the preamp's own input noise along with the signal, so on a quiet source a low-output microphone can leave audible hiss even though the microphone itself is quiet. For quiet sources, compare microphone sensitivity, its own noise and the preamp’s equivalent input noise together; a low-noise condenser often performs well. On a loud source the difference rarely matters: there is plenty of signal above the preamp's noise.

### Self-noise

A condenser's electronics produce some noise even in a silent room. **Self-noise** (or "equivalent noise level") is quoted as the SPL that would produce the same output, usually A-weighted (dB-A). Neumann specifies the U 87 Ai's self-noise as **12 dB-A** in cardioid. Below about 10 dB-A is very quiet; above about 20 dB-A can become audible on quiet sources.

Passive dynamics and ribbons have no active electronics, but their winding and transformer resistance still generate thermal noise. That noise and the preamp’s input noise both contribute to the recorded noise floor.

### Maximum SPL and dynamic range

Max SPL is the level at which distortion reaches a stated figure (often 0.5% or 1% THD). Neumann gives **117 dB SPL** for the U 87 Ai at 0.5 % THD (127 dB with its pre-attenuation pad).

The **dynamic range** is the gap between the self-noise and the max SPL. Both are already decibel levels on the same SPL scale, so the range is simply their difference: about 117 − 12 = 105 dB for the U 87 Ai in cardioid. Because the self-noise figure is A-weighted, this is an approximate, A-weighted range. The pad raises the top end to 127 dB SPL so that very loud sources do not overload the microphone's electronics.

## Key takeaways
- Sensitivity relates output voltage to acoustic pressure, commonly at one kilohertz and one pascal.
- Compare microphone noise and preamp noise together.
- Dynamic range requires both a noise reference and a stated overload criterion.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)
- [SM58 manufacturer specifications — Shure](https://pubs.shure.com/view/guide/SM58/en-US.pdf)

questions.prompt: Microphone sensitivity is conventionally quoted at which sound pressure?

options.text: 20 µPa, which is 0 dB SPL
options.explanation: That is the reference for dB SPL, far too quiet for a sensible sensitivity measurement.

options.text: 1 V
options.explanation: Volts are the output, not the acoustic input.

options.text: 114 dB SPL
options.explanation: Some calibrators produce 114 dB SPL (10 Pa), but sensitivity is normalised to 1 Pa.

options.text: 1 Pa, which is about 94 dB SPL
options.explanation: Correct. Sensitivity is quoted per pascal, normally at 1 kHz, and 1 Pa is about 94 dB SPL.

questions.workedExample:
1. Sensitivity relates output voltage to sound pressure, so it is quoted "per pascal" (mV/Pa or dBV/Pa), normally at 1 kHz.
2. 1 Pa is 50,000 times the 20 µPa reference, which is about 94 dB SPL. That is a convenient, realistic level: a loud voice close to a mic.
3. So "28 mV/Pa" means 28 mV out with a 94 dB SPL tone at 1 kHz.

Calibrators producing 94 dB SPL (or 114 dB SPL, ten times the pressure) exist for exactly this reason.

questions.prompt: You record a quiet acoustic guitar with a Neumann U 87 Ai (28 mV/Pa). You swap to a Shure SM58 (1.6 mV/Pa, about 25 dB less output) on the same preamp and raise the gain until the recorded level matches. What is the most likely difference?

options.text: None: gain raises signal and noise equally, so the result is identical
options.explanation: The preamp's own input noise is fixed. The SM58's smaller signal needs about 25 dB more gain, which lifts the preamp noise relative to the guitar.

options.text: More audible hiss, because the extra preamp gain amplifies the preamp's own input noise along with the weaker signal
options.explanation: Correct. On a quiet source, a low-output mic puts its signal closer to the preamp noise floor, so the noise in the recording rises.

options.text: The SM58 distorts, because its output is too low for the preamp
options.explanation: Low output does not cause clipping; the preamp simply needs more gain.

options.text: The recording becomes brighter, because more gain boosts high frequencies
options.explanation: Gain is applied across the whole band. The two mics do sound different, but that is their own frequency response, not the gain.

questions.workedExample:
1. Sensitivity sets how much voltage each mic produces from the same sound. The U 87 Ai gives about 17.5 times the voltage of the SM58, about 25 dB.
2. To match levels, the preamp must add about 25 dB more gain for the SM58.
3. The preamp has a fixed equivalent input noise. Raising gain lifts that noise by the same 25 dB, while the guitar only returns to the original level.
4. So the guitar sits closer to the noise floor: more hiss.

On a loud source (a guitar cab, a kick drum) there is so much signal that the difference rarely matters, which is why dynamics are fine there.

questions.prompt: Neumann specifies the U 87 Ai (cardioid) with 12 dB-A self-noise and 117 dB SPL maximum SPL without its pad. What's its approximate dynamic range?

options.text: 129 dB
options.explanation: Adding the two numbers doesn't give a range. The range is the difference.

options.text: 117 dB
options.explanation: That's the max SPL, measured from 0 dB SPL, not from the self-noise floor.

options.text: 12 dB
options.explanation: That's the self-noise alone.

options.text: 105 dB
options.explanation: Correct. 117 − 12 = 105 dB.

questions.workedExample:
1. Both figures are levels on the same dB SPL scale: the self-noise behaves like a 12 dB SPL sound, and distortion reaches 0.5 % THD at 117 dB SPL.
2. The usable range lies between them, so it is their difference: about 105 dB.
3. Adding them (129) or reading one figure alone (117 or 12) does not describe a range.

The self-noise is A-weighted, so this is an approximate, A-weighted range. With the pre-attenuation pad, the max SPL rises to 127 dB.

lessons.title: Understand phantom-power connections
lessons.summary: P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors.
lessons.body:
## Phantom power (P48)

Condenser microphones are powered through the same balanced cable that carries their signal. **IEC 61938** defines **P48**:

- **+48 V** fed through two matched **6.81 kΩ** resistors, one to each signal conductor (pins 2 and 3 of an XLR), with the shield (XLR pin 1) as the return.
- Closely matched feed resistors help preserve the impedance balance of the line.
- The standard allows up to **10 mA** per microphone. Lower-voltage P12 and P24 variants also exist.

The equal DC on the signal wires is common-mode, so it does not appear across an ideal floating dynamic coil. A preamp still needs suitable DC blocking, voltage ratings and transient protection: common-mode rejection alone does not make an arbitrary balanced input safe at 48 V.

The microphone draws its current through both feed resistors at once, so they act like a single resistor of half the value (about 3.4 kΩ). Current through a resistance drops voltage across it, so **the more current a microphone draws, the less of the 48 V reaches it**:

| Microphone current | Approximate voltage at the mic |
|---|---|
| 0.8 mA (the U 87 Ai, per Neumann) | about 45 V |
| 5 mA | about 31 V |
| 10 mA (the standard's maximum) | about 14 V |

```formula reference
V_mic = V_s − I R_feed
where
V_mic: the DC voltage left at the microphone, in volts (V)
V_s: the phantom supply voltage, 48 V for P48
I: the current the microphone draws, in amperes (A); P48 allows up to 10 mA (0.010 A)
R_feed: the combined resistance of the two 6.81 kΩ feed resistors in parallel, about 3405 ohms (Ω)
Ω: ohm, the unit of resistance
V: volt
A: ampere (amp), the unit of current
In words: The voltage at the microphone is the supply voltage minus the drop across the paralleled feed resistors, so a microphone that draws more current sees less than 48 volts.
```

So the feed resistors limit what the microphone can draw: a low-current mic sees nearly the full 48 V, while a hungry one sees much less. A supply or interface that can't deliver enough current makes some microphones distort earlier or lose headroom, so check the microphone's stated current against the interface's phantom specification.

> [!warning] Phantom power and your synth
> As module 5 said, keep phantom **off** on any channel your synth or other line-level gear is plugged into. Phantom is for microphones and DI boxes designed for it.

## Key takeaways
- P48 uses matched feed resistors to apply common-mode DC to the signal conductors.
- Feed resistance makes the microphone’s connector voltage depend on current draw.
- Use compatible inputs and correct cables; turn phantom off for equipment that does not require it.

## Further reading
- [Phantom supply and XLR contact diagrams — Schoeps CMC/MK manual, October 2015](https://schoeps.de/fileadmin/user_upload/user_upload/Downloads/Bedienungsanleitungen/SCHOEPS_Manual_CMC_MK_E_2015-10-03_1444311033__1_.pdf)
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)
- [Ribbon microphone phantom precautions — Royer](https://royerlabs.com/faqs/)

questions.prompt: Which statements about IEC 61938 P48 phantom power are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: The standard allows up to 10 mA per microphone
options.explanation: Correct.

options.text: Phantom appears as a 48 V difference between XLR pin 2 and XLR pin 3
options.explanation: Phantom DC is common-mode on the two signal legs. A phantom-compatible input needs appropriate DC blocking and protection; differential amplification alone does not provide voltage tolerance.

options.text: +48 V is applied equally to XLR pins 2 and 3 through matched 6.81 kΩ resistors
options.explanation: Correct. That's the P48 definition.

options.text: The shield (XLR pin 1) is the return path
options.explanation: Correct. Interrupting the actual microphone pin-1 return breaks this circuit, but a DI ground-lift switch may preserve its phantom return.

questions.workedExample:
```
+48V --6.81k--> pin 2
+48V --6.81k--> pin 3
0 V  ----------> pin 1 (shield)
```

The DC is common-mode and does not appear across an ideal floating coil. The input must still be designed to tolerate and block phantom DC and transients. The mic draws its current through both resistors in parallel (3.4 kΩ).

questions.prompt: You're about to plug a vintage passive ribbon mic into a channel that has phantom power available. Which precautions are sensible? Select all that apply.

options.text: Check the cable is correctly wired, for example no short from XLR pin 1 to XLR pin 2 or XLR pin 3
options.explanation: Correct. A fault can put phantom voltage across the mic's output.

options.text: Use an XLR-to-TS unbalanced adapter so phantom can't reach the mic
options.explanation: An unbalanced adapter typically ties one signal leg to ground, which with phantom on can put DC across the mic. It's one of the known damage routes.

options.text: Switch phantom off on that channel before connecting
options.explanation: Correct. Good practice for anything that doesn't need phantom.

options.text: Avoid hot-plugging into a live phantom input
options.explanation: Correct. Pins make contact at different instants, which can put a transient across the ribbon or preamp.

questions.workedExample:
With a correctly wired balanced cable, both signal contacts carry equal phantom DC, so an ideal floating passive output sees no differential DC. Schoeps recommends connecting microphones with phantom switched off; Royer also warns about miswired cables and live patch-bay connections.

1. Check that XLR pin 1 is the shield/phantom return and that XLR pin 2 and XLR pin 3 are the signal contacts, without faults between them.
2. Avoid unbalanced adapters that connect a signal leg to the return.
3. Switch phantom off, allow the interface's specified discharge time, and connect using the microphone maker's procedure.

A differential input still needs suitable DC blocking, component voltage ratings and transient protection.

lessons.title: Control leakage and comb filtering
lessons.summary: Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage.
lessons.body:
## Placement basics

- **Distance controls the direct-to-room balance.** Close placement gives more direct sound, less room, more proximity effect and more level variation as the performer moves. Further away captures more of the room.
- **Angle controls tone.** On a guitar cab, the centre of the cone is brighter; towards the edge it's darker. Small moves matter.
- Use **acoustic nulls**. Aim the null of a directional mic at what you *don't* want (a monitor, a neighbouring drum).
- Mind **sound reflections**. A music stand or desk near the mic adds a reflection a few milliseconds late, which comb-filters the sound.

### The 3:1 rule

When several mics are open at once, a source reaches its own mic and, more weakly and later, its neighbours. When the signals are mixed, the delayed copy comb-filters the direct one. The **3:1 rule** says the distance *between* mics should be at least **three times** the distance from each mic to its source.

Why it works: by the inverse square law, sound pressure falls in proportion to distance. A neighbouring mic three times further away picks up the source about **9.5 dB** quieter than its own mic does (assuming similar pickup and channel gains).

```formula reference
L_leak = 20 log_10(d_far / d_near)
where
L_leak: how far the leaked copy is below the direct sound, in decibels (dB)
d_far: the distance from the source to the neighbouring mic, in metres (m)
d_near: the distance from the source to its own mic, in metres (m)
log_10: the base-10 logarithm; 20 × log_10 because pressure is an amplitude
dB: decibel
m: metre
In words: The leaked copy is quieter than the direct sound by 20 times the logarithm of how many times further away the neighbouring mic is; three times further gives about 9.5 dB.
```

A copy that much quieter cannot cancel or double the direct sound. Mixed in, it can only nudge the sum: the comb filter's peaks are about +2.5 dB and its notches about −3.5 dB, instead of the +6 dB peaks and deep notches of two equal copies. The comb is still there, but shallow enough that it is rarely objectionable. The quieter the leak, the shallower the comb.

```diagram
  src A      src B
   |          |
  0.3 m      0.3 m
   |          |
  mic A ---- mic B
     >= 0.9 m apart
```

It's a rule of thumb that assumes omni-like pickup and similar levels. Directional mics aimed well, or very different source levels, change the numbers.

## Key takeaways
- Distance changes direct-to-room balance and leakage.
- The three-to-one spacing rule is a practical starting estimate.
- Leakage ripple also depends on source geometry, microphone response and channel gains.

## Further reading
- [Microphone technology — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/mic-university/technology/microphone-technology-the-essentials/)
- [U 87 Ai technical data — Neumann](https://www.neumann.com/en-en/products/microphones/u-87-ai/)
- [Phantom power — Schoeps](https://schoeps.de/en/knowledge/knowledge-base/technical-basics/phantom-power-p48p12.html)
- [Three-to-one rule — DPA](https://www.dpamicrophones.com/dict/3-1-rule/)

questions.prompt: Two cardioid mics are each 25 cm from their own singers. Following the 3:1 rule, what's the minimum spacing between the mics?

options.text: 75 cm
options.explanation: Correct. 3 × 25 cm = 75 cm.

options.text: 25 cm
options.explanation: This does not satisfy the rule. Actual leakage also depends on geometry, polar patterns and channel gains.

options.text: 50 cm
options.explanation: That's 2:1; the rule asks for 3:1.

options.text: 8.3 cm
options.explanation: That divides by three instead of multiplying.

questions.workedExample:
1. The 3:1 rule: the spacing between mics should be at least three times each mic's distance from its own source.
2. 3 × 25 cm = 75 cm.
3. At that spacing, each singer is about three times further from the other mic, so the leakage arrives roughly 9.5 dB quieter. A copy that much quieter only makes shallow comb filtering (a few dB).

The rule assumes similar channel gains and pickup. Cardioids aimed with their rear null towards the other singer reduce leakage further.

questions.prompt: Two mics pick up a broadband source; the second mic's copy is delayed. At first the leaked copy is only slightly quieter than the direct sound, and the mix sounds hollow and phasey. You move the second mic until the leak is about 9.5 dB below the direct sound, keeping equal channel gains. What happens to the comb filtering?

options.text: The peaks and notches become shallow, roughly +2.5 dB and −3.5 dB, but do not disappear
options.explanation: Correct. A quieter copy can only nudge the sum up or down. The comb remains, but much shallower than with nearly equal copies.

options.text: It disappears completely
options.explanation: Any nonzero delayed copy still produces a comb in this model; it just becomes shallower.

options.text: The notches get deeper, because the copy now arrives later
options.explanation: The delay sets where the notches fall in frequency. Their depth is set by how close in level the two copies are.

options.text: The peaks and notches swing by about ±9.5 dB
options.explanation: The ripple is much smaller than the level difference: a copy at about a third of the amplitude adds or subtracts only a little.

questions.workedExample:
1. Mixing a direct sound with a delayed copy produces peaks where they arrive in phase and notches where they arrive out of phase.
2. With nearly equal copies, peaks approach +6 dB and notches become very deep: the hollow sound.
3. With the copy about 9.5 dB down (about a third of the amplitude), the sum can only range from about two-thirds to about four-thirds of the direct sound: roughly −3.5 dB to +2.5 dB.
4. Moving the mic also changes the delay, which shifts where the notches fall, but their depth is controlled by the level difference.

This is the reasoning behind the 3:1 rule.

lessons.title: From voice-coil current to cone force
lessons.summary: A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force.
lessons.body:
A **loudspeaker driver** is the motor and diaphragm that actually move air. A loudspeaker *system* is one or more drivers plus an enclosure (the enclosure units) and usually a crossover (the crossover units). This lesson is about the driver: how it works, and how to read the numbers on its datasheet.

## The motor structure

Nearly all speakers you will meet are **moving-coil** (electrodynamic) drivers, a design dating from the 1920s.

```diagram
     surround          cone
   ,-----------.  /
  (             )/
   \  +-------+ /      spider
    \ | coil  |/  ===  (suspension)
  [N]=|=gap===|=[N]
  [S]  pole    [S]  <- magnet
       piece
```

The parts:

- **Magnet and pole pieces (the motor).** A permanent magnet (ferrite or neodymium) and steel parts concentrate a strong magnetic field in a narrow ring-shaped **magnetic gap**.
- **Voice coil.** A coil of fine wire wound on a light former, sitting in the gap. It's attached to the cone.
- **Cone (diaphragm).** Pushes the air. Paper, polypropylene, aluminium and composites are common. It must be light and stiff.
- **Driver suspension.** The **driver surround** at the outer edge and the **driver spider** behind the cone keep the coil centred in the gap and provide a restoring force that pulls the cone back to rest.
- **Basket (frame)** holds it all together.

## How current becomes sound

A current in a wire in a magnetic field feels a force (the Lorentz force; it's the motor principle). The voice coil is wound so the wire crosses the field at right angles everywhere in the gap, so the force on it is simply:

```formula essential
F = Bl i
where
F: the force on the voice coil (and so on the cone), in newtons (N)
B: the magnetic flux density in the gap, how strong the magnet's field is there, in tesla (T); around 1 T is typical
l: the length of voice-coil wire sitting in the field, in metres (m); often several metres of fine wire
i: the current through the voice coil, in amperes (A)
Bl: the product of B and l, quoted on datasheets as the "force factor" or "BL", in tesla-metres (T·m); typically about 5–20 T·m
N: newton, the unit of force
T: tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density
m: metre
A: ampere, the unit of current
In words: the push on the cone is proportional to the current in this small-signal model; a stronger field or more wire in the gap gives more push per amp.
```

Datasheets quote the product **Bl** ("BL") because B and l only ever appear together. A 7 T·m driver turns each ampere into about 7 newtons of push. Three consequences follow:

- **The force follows the current**, not the voltage. The amplifier sets a voltage; the driver's impedance (next lesson) decides how much current flows.
- **Audio current alternates, so the force alternates** and the cone moves back and forth, pushing air (the acoustics lessons).
- **The relationship is only linear while the coil stays in the gap.** At large excursions part of the coil leaves the strongest field, so Bl falls and the force no longer follows the current: one source of distortion at high level (a later lesson covers excursion limits).

The cone, coil and the air it carries have **mass**; the surround and spider act as a **suspension spring**. Mass on a spring has a resonance. That's the driver's **free-air resonance, Fs**, one of the Thiele–Small parameters in the enclosure lessons. A heavier cone or a softer suspension lowers Fs. Below Fs the output falls away.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a weight on a rubber band
> Hang a weight from a rubber band and flick it: it bounces at its own natural rate. A heavier weight or a floppier band bounces more slowly. Jiggle your hand slowly and the weight just follows; jiggle near its natural rate and it swings wildly.
>
> **How it maps:** The weight is the moving mass of the cone, coil and air load; the rubber band is the suspension's springiness; the natural bounce rate is Fs. The motor's force is your hand driving the system.
>
> **Where it stops:** A driver's resonance is strongly damped, partly by the suspension and largely by the motor and amplifier acting electrically, so it does not ring on like a bouncing weight. In a box, the trapped air adds a second spring and raises the resonance.

A driver is also an **electromagnetic generator**: a moving coil in a field produces a voltage (back-EMF), exactly as a dynamic mic does. That back-EMF is why the impedance changes so much near resonance.

## Key takeaways
- A magnetic field and current-carrying voice coil create force.
- Moving mass and suspension compliance establish the driver’s free-air resonance.
- The moving coil also generates back electromotive force.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

questions.prompt: In a moving-coil driver, what produces the force that moves the cone?

options.text: Current in the voice coil sitting in the magnet's field
options.explanation: Correct. A current in a conductor in a magnetic field feels a force proportional to B, wire length and current.

options.text: The magnet attracting the cone directly
options.explanation: The cone isn't magnetic. The force acts on the current-carrying voice coil.

options.text: Air pressure from the enclosure
options.explanation: The enclosure's air acts as a spring on the cone, but it isn't the driving force.

options.text: Electric charge pulling the cone towards a fixed plate
options.explanation: Electrostatic loudspeakers use electric forces between charged structures. A moving-coil driver's motor instead uses current in a magnetic field.

questions.workedExample:
1. The motor concentrates a magnetic field in a narrow gap.
2. The voice coil sits in the gap and is attached to the cone.
3. Amplifier current through the coil produces a force proportional to the field strength, the length of wire in the field and the current: the datasheet's force factor Bl times the current.
4. Alternating current gives an alternating force, so the cone vibrates and pushes air.

The cone itself is not magnetic, and the enclosure's air acts as a spring that resists the motion rather than driving it.

lessons.title: Read a driver’s impedance curve
lessons.summary: An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency.
lessons.body:
## Impedance: nominal vs reality

An "8 Ω" speaker isn't 8 Ω. Its impedance depends on frequency:

- At DC it's just the voice-coil resistance, **Re** (often around 5–7 Ω for an "8 Ω" driver).
- Near **Fs** it rises to a sharp peak, because the back-EMF of the resonating cone opposes the current.
- Above resonance it falls to a minimum, then rises again at high frequencies because the voice coil is an **inductor**.

A simple electrical model adds up three parts: the coil's resistance, the coil’s inductive impedance (which grows with frequency), and a "motional" part caused by the cone's movement, which peaks at resonance. Impedance is really a complex number, because it also shifts the timing (phase) of the current; the *size* of the total is what an impedance plot shows.

Purdue's sample woofer (6.6 Ω coil resistance, 0.48 mH inductance, 65 Hz free-air resonance, electrical Q of 0.436 and mechanical Q of 2.25) shows how much the size varies in that simple model:

| Frequency | Approximate impedance |
|---|---|
| 20 Hz | 8.9 Ω |
| 65 Hz (Fs) | 40.7 Ω |
| 200 Hz | 8.9 Ω |
| 600 Hz | 6.7 Ω |
| 2 kHz | 8.6 Ω |
| 10 kHz | 30.8 Ω |

From 6.7 Ω to over 40 Ω across the band. Real voice-coil inductance is lossy, so the high-frequency rise is usually gentler than this simple model shows.

The resonance peak's height depends on how the resonance is damped. A lightly damped suspension (high mechanical Q) gives a tall, sharp peak and a lossy suspension (low mechanical Q) a lower, broader one. A stronger motor, which has a lower electrical Q, makes the peak taller still, because the moving coil generates more back-EMF. This is also how Fs and the two Qs are measured: from the shape of the impedance curve.

```formula reference
Z_max = R_e (1 + Q_ms / Q_es)
where
Z_max: the impedance at the resonance peak, in ohms (Ω), neglecting voice-coil inductance
R_e: the voice coil's DC resistance (Re on datasheets), in ohms (Ω)
Q_ms: the mechanical Q (Qms): how sharp the resonance is from suspension losses alone; a pure number, roughly 0.5–10 and often about 3
Q_es: the electrical Q (Qes): how strongly the motor's electrical damping controls the resonance; a pure number, typically about 0.2–1
Ω: ohm, the unit of impedance and resistance
In words: The resonance peak is the coil resistance multiplied up by one plus the ratio of the mechanical Q to the electrical Q, so a sharper mechanical resonance gives a taller peak; the Purdue sample reaches about 41 ohms.
```

**Nominal impedance** is a single rounded label for the region above resonance. The loudspeaker standard IEC 60268-5 says the minimum impedance in the rated frequency range should not fall below **80% of the rated (nominal) impedance**: an "8 Ω" speaker should not dip below 6.4 Ω in its working range. Not every manufacturer follows that rule, and real multi-way speakers with crossovers can dip well below their label, which is why amplifier makers care about the *minimum*, not the nominal (the power-amplifier lessons).

## Key takeaways
- An impedance label does not mean constant impedance at every frequency.
- Resonance, coil resistance and inductance shape the curve.
- Amplifier compatibility requires the load’s magnitude and phase, not just its nominal label.

lessons.title: Compare speaker sensitivity references
lessons.summary: Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts.
lessons.body:
## Sensitivity and the maths of power vs SPL

**Loudspeaker sensitivity** is the SPL on-axis at 1 m for a reference input. Two conventions:

- **dB SPL @ 1 W / 1 m.** One watt into the *nominal* impedance.
- **dB SPL @ 2.83 V / 1 m.** 2.83 V is 1 W into 8 Ω.

Why 2.83 V? Into a plain resistance, the power a voltage delivers is the voltage squared divided by the resistance, so 2.83 V into 8 Ω is almost exactly 1 W.

```formula reference
P = V^2 / R
where
P: the electrical power delivered, in watts (W)
V: the RMS voltage across the speaker, in volts (V)
R: the load's (nominal) impedance, treated as a plain resistance, in ohms (Ω)
W: watt, the unit of power
Ω: ohm
In words: Power is voltage squared divided by resistance, so a fixed voltage pushes twice the power into half the resistance: 2.83 volts is 1 watt into 8 ohms but 2 watts into 4 ohms.
```

Using nominal impedance to define the test voltage, the two references agree for 8 Ω. For a **4 Ω** speaker, the same 2.83 V pushes twice the current and **2 W nominal**. Doubling the power adds about 3 dB (the next lesson), so a 4 Ω speaker's voltage-sensitivity figure looks about **3 dB higher** than its 1 W figure. It is not a more efficient speaker; it is simply drawing more power from the amplifier at that voltage.

So before comparing two speakers, convert both figures to the same reference. Actual electrical power also varies with the complex impedance at each frequency, so check the measurement conditions too.

## Key takeaways
- Check whether sensitivity is referred to one watt or 2.83 volts.
- The voltage reference corresponds to about one watt nominal into eight ohms, and two into four ohms.
- In the linear regime, doubling power gives approximately three decibels.

## Further reading

- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

2. 2 W is double the power.

4. 90 dB + 3 dB ≈ 93 dB SPL.

Doubling the voltage into the same load is four times the power, which would give about +6 dB.

2. The same 2.83 V across a 4 Ω speaker drives twice the current and so twice the power: about 2 W.
3. So speaker B uses about 2 W to make 88 dB. With 1 W it would make about 3 dB less: about 85 dB at 1 W / 1 m.
4. Speaker A makes 88 dB with 1 W, so it is about 3 dB more sensitive per watt.

lessons.title: Work backwards from required listener level
lessons.summary: Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction.
lessons.body:
## Power, distance and efficiency

To predict how loud a speaker will be, start from its sensitivity, add the decibels gained by using more than 1 W, and subtract the decibels lost by listening further away than 1 m. For a fixed signal spectrum in the linear range, use this approximate on-axis free-field, far-field estimate (neglecting air absorption and power compression):

```formula reference
SPL = S + 10 log_10(P / 1 W)
      − 20 log_10(r / 1 m)
where
SPL: the sound pressure level at the listener, in decibels (dB SPL)
S: the speaker's sensitivity, in dB SPL at 1 W / 1 m; typically 84–90 dB for hi-fi, over 100 dB for PA horns
P: the amplifier power into the speaker's nominal impedance, in watts (W)
r: the listening distance from the speaker, in metres (m); in the actual source’s far field; one metre is a reference distance, not a universal far-field boundary
log_10: the base-10 logarithm
W: watt
m: metre
dB: decibel
In words: Start from the speaker's sensitivity at 1 watt and 1 metre, add about 3 dB for every doubling of amplifier power and subtract about 6 dB for every doubling of listening distance.
```

The two terms behave very differently, and that asymmetry is the whole lesson:

- **Power buys level slowly.** Each **doubling of power adds only 3 dB**; ten times the power adds 10 dB. An 87 dB/1 W/1 m speaker gives about 97 dB at 1 m with 10 W and about 107 dB with 100 W.
- **Distance takes level away quickly.** Each doubling of distance costs about 6 dB, so moving the audience twice as far away needs **four times** the power to keep the same level.
- **Sensitivity is cheap power.** Every 3 dB of extra sensitivity halves the amplifier power needed for the same level; 6 dB quarters it.

Worked example (from Purdue's notes), reasoning backwards from the listener: you want 90 dB SPL at 4 m outdoors from an 86 dB/1 W/1 m speaker.

1. 4 m is two doublings of 1 m, which costs about 12 dB. So you need about 102 dB at 1 m.
2. That is 16 dB above the speaker's 1 W figure.
3. 16 dB is a power ratio of about 40 (10 dB is ×10, and each further 3 dB roughly doubles it). So about **40 W**.

That 40 W is an *average* power for a steady signal. Music has peaks well above its average: a signal whose peaks are 10 dB above its RMS level (a 10 dB crest factor) needs about ten times the average power at each peak. An amplifier sized only for the average will clip on every drum hit, so leave headroom while respecting the driver's excursion and thermal limits (the amplifier lessons).

Sensitivity is closely related to **loudspeaker efficiency**, the fraction of electrical power that comes out as sound. Typical home loudspeakers are only around 1 % efficient, and often less: Purdue's sample driver, rated 86 dB/1 W/1 m, works out at about 0.2 %, so of that 40 W only around a tenth of a watt leaves as sound. The rest becomes heat, mostly in the voice coil, which is why high power heats the coil and raises its resistance (power compression).

## Key takeaways
- Use a consistent reference, spectrum and far-field measurement direction.
- Distance loss can demand much more power than a sensitivity comparison alone suggests.
- Leave appropriate peak margin while respecting driver excursion and thermal limits.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

options.explanation: Doubling the power adds only about 3 dB, but doubling the distance costs about 6 dB.

options.text: About 200 W
options.explanation: Correct. Twice the distance costs about 6 dB, and 6 dB is two doublings of power: four times 50 W.

2. To win back 6 dB with power alone, remember each doubling of power adds about 3 dB, so 6 dB needs two doublings: four times the power.
3. 4 × 50 W = 200 W.

This is why distance is expensive. Before buying the power, check the speaker's thermal and excursion limits; adding a second speaker or a delay speaker closer to the audience is often better.

The level is right on sustained notes, but drum hits sound harsh and the amplifier's clip light keeps lighting. The music's peaks are about 10 dB above its average. What went wrong?

2. Music's peaks are higher. With peaks about 10 dB above the average, each peak needs about ten times the power for an instant.

4. Choose an amplifier with clean peak capability well above the average, then use limiting and the driver's thermal and excursion limits to keep the system safe.

lessons.title: Driver response, dispersion and limits
lessons.summary: A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency.
lessons.body:
## Frequency response

A frequency response plot shows on-axis SPL (at a fixed input) against frequency. Look for:

- The **usable range**, often given as ±3 dB limits, with the low-frequency limit set mainly by Fs and the enclosure.
- **Smoothness**: narrow peaks often come from cone breakup or cabinet resonance.
- **Off-axis curves**: how the response changes at 30° or 60°. Because of diffraction, a driver radiates widely when its wavelength is large compared with the cone, and shows **beaming** (narrower dispersion) when the wavelength becomes comparable with the cone.

Where does beaming start? Treat the cone as a flat, rigid disc (a "piston"). Directivity becomes significant roughly when the cone's circumference reaches one wavelength. So the bigger the cone, the lower the frequency at which it starts beaming: double the radius and beaming starts an octave lower.

```formula reference
f_beam = c / (2πa)
where
f_beam: the frequency above which the cone starts to focus sound forwards instead of spreading it, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
π: pi, about 3.14159
a: the effective radius of the cone (half its effective diameter), in metres (m)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: In the rigid-piston model, beaming becomes significant when the cone's circumference is about one wavelength, so a cone of twice the radius starts beaming an octave lower.
```

For a woofer with a 13 cm effective diameter this gives about 840 Hz; for a 25 mm tweeter dome, about 4.4 kHz, roughly five times higher because the dome is roughly five times smaller. The piston model stops being reliable once the cone breaks up (below), so check measured off-axis curves.

That beaming is one reason multi-way speakers hand high frequencies to smaller drivers.

## Power handling

Two separate limits:

- **Driver power handling** (thermal). The voice coil heats up. Too much *average* power for too long burns the coil or its adhesive. Ratings are usually based on long tests with band-limited noise, and the method (and so the number) differs between standards and manufacturers, so read what method a figure refers to.
- **Mechanical (excursion).** At low frequencies the cone must move a long way. **Xmax** describes an excursion limit under a specified geometric or distortion criterion; definitions vary. Motor, suspension and other nonlinearities can limit it. Beyond the useful linear range, distortion increases; far beyond it, the coil can strike the motor structure or the suspension can tear. A driver can be over-excursed at low frequencies with modest power, especially below a ported box's tuning frequency (the enclosure units).

> [!tip] Power ratings are not targets
> A "100 W" speaker doesn't need 100 W, and isn't safe with any 100 W signal. A clipped signal from a small amplifier can damage a tweeter (the power-amplifier units), while the required clean peak capacity and suitable protection must be chosen from actual limits.

## Driver types

| Driver | Typical job | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Subwoofer | Below ~80–120 Hz | Long excursion, big cone |
| Woofer | Bass (and mids in 2-way) | 13–38 cm common |
| Midrange | ~300 Hz–3 kHz | Covers the vocal region |
| Tweeter | Above ~2–3 kHz | Light dome, 19–28 mm |
| Compression driver + horn | Mid/high in PA | Very high sensitivity |

In a **compression driver**, a diaphragm pressurises a small chamber; sound passes through **phase-plug** channels into a narrow **horn throat**, and the **loudspeaker horn** flares out to the room. The horn improves the match between the diaphragm and the air, so far more of the electrical power becomes sound. It also controls dispersion, which PA designers use to aim sound at the audience and away from walls. Horn-loaded systems can reach sensitivities around 110 dB SPL at 2.83 V/1 m; a typical hi-fi speaker is in the mid-80s to around 90 dB.

## Cone breakup

At low frequencies a cone moves as a rigid **rigid piston**. As frequency rises, the cone stops moving as one piece: bending waves travel across it, and different parts move with different phase. This is **cone breakup**. It causes:

- Peaks and dips in the response, often a sharp peak near the top of the driver's range.
- Changes in dispersion, and sometimes audible coloration and distortion.

Stiff, light cones (aluminium, ceramic) push breakup higher but often produce a stronger, sharper peak when it happens. Softer, well-damped cones break up earlier but more gently. Either way, the crossover (the crossover units) is chosen so the driver isn't asked to play much in its breakup region.

## Key takeaways
- A larger piston becomes directional at a lower frequency.
- Cone breakup invalidates a rigid-piston prediction; use measured off-axis data.
- Thermal power and cone excursion are separate limits.
- Driver types trade displacement, bandwidth, dispersion and efficiency.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Baffled piston radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/BaffledPiston/BaffledPiston.html)
- [Rated impedance — Dynaudio](https://dynaudio.com/magazine/2023/july/impedance-ask-the-expert)

options.text: At about 840 Hz too: beaming depends only on frequency
options.explanation: Beaming depends on the driver's size compared with the wavelength, so a smaller driver beams at a higher frequency.

options.text: Much lower, around 170 Hz
options.explanation: That gets the direction backwards. A smaller driver needs a shorter wavelength, which is a higher frequency, before it beams.

options.text: It never beams at audible frequencies
options.explanation: Every finite piston beams once the wavelength becomes comparable with its size; a small dome just does so higher up.

2. A 25 mm dome is roughly a fifth of a 13 cm cone's diameter.

4. That is why the tweeter takes over above a few kilohertz: it keeps dispersion wide where the woofer would beam.

questions.prompt: Which are genuine ways a driver can be damaged or driven into gross distortion? Select all that apply.

options.text: Too much average power overheating the voice coil
options.explanation: Correct. That's the thermal limit.

options.text: Excessive cone excursion at low frequencies beyond Xmax
options.explanation: Correct. That's the mechanical limit; it can happen at modest power at low frequencies.

options.text: Reducing the input while keeping the signal within every applicable thermal and excursion limit
options.explanation: Operating within all applicable limits does not itself cause overload. A power number alone is not enough to establish those limits.

options.text: Sustained heavy clipping that adds high-frequency energy, especially for tweeters
options.explanation: Correct. Clipping adds harmonics and raises average power, which can overheat a tweeter.

questions.workedExample:
Two independent limits:

1. **Thermal**: the voice coil heats with average power. Long, loud, compressed or clipped signals push it.
2. **Mechanical**: excursion grows as frequency falls (for the same SPL). Beyond Xmax, distortion rises; well beyond, the coil can bottom out.

Clipping matters for tweeters because it adds high-frequency harmonics that the crossover passes straight to them (the power-amplifier units).

questions.prompt: A frequency response plot of a 16 cm aluminium-cone woofer shows a sharp +8 dB peak at 5 kHz. Which statements are likely true? Select all that apply.

options.text: The peak means the woofer will play bass better
options.explanation: Breakup is a high-frequency effect and doesn't help low-frequency output.

options.text: A rigid-piston model predicts narrowing at 5 kHz, but breakup makes actual off-axis measurements necessary
options.explanation: Correct. The rigid-piston beaming point for a 13 cm effective diameter is near 840 Hz. Above breakup, the rigid-piston approximation no longer predicts the actual radiation reliably.

options.text: The peak is probably cone breakup: the cone has stopped behaving as a rigid piston
options.explanation: Correct. Stiff metal cones tend to show a sharp breakup peak near the top of their range.

options.text: A crossover that lets the woofer play up to 4–5 kHz at full level would expose that peak
options.explanation: Correct. The crossover should roll the woofer off well below its breakup region.

1. Breakup: bending waves cross the cone and parts move out of phase. Stiff, light cones break up high but with sharp peaks, like this +8 dB peak at 5 kHz.
2. Directivity: the rigid-piston model already predicts this woofer narrowing from roughly 840 Hz, far below its 5 kHz peak. Above breakup the model no longer describes the radiation, so measured polar data is needed.
3. A sharp breakup peak does nothing for bass.
4. Both points say the same thing: cross over to a tweeter well below 5 kHz, often around 2–3 kHz for this size, with a slope steep enough to suppress the peak.

lessons.title: Separate front and rear radiation
lessons.summary: A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies.
lessons.body:
Hold a bare woofer in the air, play a bass line through it, and you get a thin, tinny sound. Mount the same driver in a box and the bass appears. This lesson explains why, and how the box's design shapes the bass response.

It's a deep subject with decades of published theory. The goal here is the concepts you need to read a driver datasheet and understand what box-modelling software tells you.

## The acoustic short circuit

When the cone moves forward, it compresses the air in front and rarefies the air behind. The two sides radiate **equal and opposite** pressure waves: the bare driver is a **dipole** (Dan Russell's radiation demo in Further reading shows the field).

At high frequencies the wavelength is short compared with the path from front to back around the cone's edge, so the two waves don't meet in time to cancel much. At low frequencies the wavelength is long, the rear wave easily diffracts round the edge, and it **cancels the front wave**. Air just sloshes from front to back. This is the **acoustic short circuit**, and it's why a bare driver has almost no bass.

```diagram
 bare driver:   front (+)  )  (  rear (-)
                 \_ air sloshes round _/
 on a baffle:   front (+) |  rear (-)
                  longer path, less cancel
```

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a paddle in a pond
> Push a small paddle slowly back and forth in a pond and very little water goes anywhere: it just swirls round the paddle's edges from the high side to the low side. Fix the paddle in a wide wall, or put it in a pipe, and the water has to move along instead.
>
> **How it maps:** The paddle is the cone, the water swirling round its edge is the air sloshing from the compressed front to the rarefied back, and the wall or pipe is the baffle or box that stops the short circuit. Slow strokes correspond to low frequencies, where there is plenty of time for the swirl.
>
> **Where it stops:** Water barely compresses, but air does: the air sealed in a box acts as a spring on the cone. And at high frequencies sound has no time to get round the edge at all, which is why a bare driver still has treble.

The cure is to separate front from back:

- A **baffle** (a flat board) lengthens the path, so cancellation starts at a lower frequency.
- An **enclosure** (a box) traps the rear wave completely, or redirects it so it helps.

## Baffle step

Even in a box, the front baffle has a finite size. At high frequencies, where the baffle is large compared with the wavelength, the driver radiates into the **half-space** in front: half a sphere of directions. At low frequencies, where the wavelength is much larger than the baffle, sound diffracts around the cabinet and radiates into the **full space**: the whole sphere.

Engineers often call these "2π" and "4π" radiation, after the solid angle (in steradians) that half a sphere and a whole sphere cover.

For the same cone motion, radiating into half-space gives twice the on-axis sound pressure of full space: the baffle acts like a mirror, adding a coherent "image" source. Doubling pressure is a rise of about 6 dB.

So as frequency falls and the radiation spreads into full space, a speaker's on-axis response steps down by up to **6 dB** going from high to low frequencies. The transition happens where the wavelength is comparable with the baffle width: a few hundred hertz for a typical bookshelf speaker. This is the ideal figure: the real step is smoother, and nearby walls and floors change it.

Designers compensate with **baffle step compensation**: usually a gentle shelf in the crossover that reduces everything above the step. In a real room, placing the speaker near a wall gives back some of the lost bass, which is why compensation is a judgement call.

## Key takeaways
- A bare driver has dipole cancellation at low frequencies.
- A baffle separates the front and rear paths.
- For fixed cone motion, a finite baffle can produce an approximately six-decibel transition; boundary placement changes it.

lessons.summary: Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes.
lessons.body:
## Four ways to box a driver

### Sealed (closed box, acoustic suspension)

The rear wave is trapped. The air inside acts as an extra **air spring** on the cone, which raises the system resonance above the driver's free-air Fs.

- Below the system resonance, Fc, the response falls at **12 dB per octave** (a second-order high-pass).
- Transient behaviour depends on system Q. Sealed boxes are relatively simple to model, and the trapped air adds restoring force at very low frequencies.
- Less efficient in the bass than a ported box of the same size.

### Ported (bass reflex, vented)

A **port tube** (tube) connects the box air to the outside. The air in the port is a mass, the air in the box is a spring: a **Helmholtz resonator**, tuned to a frequency Fb. Around Fb, the port radiates strongly and in phase with the cone's front, adding bass output while the cone barely moves.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: blowing across a bottle
> Blow across the neck of an empty bottle and it hoots at one pitch. The air in the neck bounces in and out on the springy air in the body. A bigger bottle or a longer, narrower neck gives a lower note.
>
> **How it maps:** The bottle is exactly the kind of resonator a port makes: the port's air is the neck's moving mass, the box air is the body's spring, and the hoot's pitch is the tuning frequency Fb. In a speaker the cone drives the resonator from inside instead of your breath from outside.
>
> **Where it stops:** A bottle's hoot is the whole point; a port is meant to add smooth bass around Fb, not a tone of its own. If the port's air moves too fast it chuffs, and below Fb the resonance stops helping and the cone is left unloaded.

- More bass extension or output from the same box volume than sealed.
- Below Fb the response falls at **24 dB per octave** (fourth-order), steeper than sealed.
- **Below Fb the box provides progressively less air-spring loading on the cone**: the suspension and motor still act, but the port increasingly relieves box pressure, so excursion can become excessive. Many ported systems use a subsonic high-pass filter to protect the driver.
- Ports can make noise ("chuffing") if the air speed is too high, usually because the port is too narrow for the output.

### Open baffle

No box at all: the driver sits on a flat panel, open at the back. It stays a **dipole**, radiating front and back with opposite polarity and a null at the sides.

- No box resonances; many listeners like the spacious presentation.
- Front-to-back cancellation adds about **6 dB per octave** of low-frequency roll-off relative to monopole radiation. The driver’s own response also matters: below its mechanical resonance, an unequalised ideal voltage-driven dipole can approach **18 dB per octave** in total. Large baffles, displacement capability and EQ may be needed.
- The rear wave reflects off the wall behind, so placement matters even more.

### Transmission line

The rear wave travels down a long, folded, damped duct before leaving through a vent. The line length is typically chosen as a **quarter wavelength** at the lowest frequency the design targets (often near the driver's resonance), so the line's output reinforces the front at low frequencies while the damping absorbs higher frequencies.

A quarter of a 40 Hz wavelength is about 2.1 m, which is why lines are folded inside the cabinet.

That is a starting estimate: stuffing slows the sound in the line and tapered lines behave differently, so real lines are tuned in modelling software. They're more complex to design and build than sealed or ported boxes.

| Type | Roll-off | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Sealed | 12 dB/oct | Compact, controlled |
| Ported | 24 dB/oct | More output; excursion below Fb |
| Open baffle | Additional ~6 dB/oct dipole loss | Driver roll-off also contributes |
| Transmission line | varies | Complex build |

## Key takeaways
- Ideal sealed and ported boxes have different low-frequency asymptotes.
- A port reduces cone movement near tuning but unloads it progressively below tuning.
- Open baffles and damped transmission lines use rear radiation differently.

lessons.title: Read the driver’s small-signal parameters
lessons.summary: Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance.
lessons.body:
## Thiele–Small parameters

A driver datasheet lists **Thiele–Small (T/S) parameters**, measured at low levels where the driver behaves linearly. The three you use most:

- **Fs**: the free-air resonance (moving mass on the suspension spring).
- **Qts**: the total Q at Fs: how damped the resonance is. Purdue's notes put most drivers between about 0.2 and 0.5.
- **Vas**: the volume of air with the same springiness (compliance) as the driver's suspension.

### Fs: a mass on a spring

The cone, voice coil and the air they carry are a mass; the surround and spider are a spring. Like any mass on a spring, they have one natural frequency. A heavier cone or a softer suspension gives a lower resonance: four times the mass halves Fs. For example, a 20 g moving mass on a suspension that moves 1 mm per newton resonates at about 36 Hz.

```formula reference
Fs = 1 / (2π √(Mms Cms))
where
Fs: the driver's free-air resonance frequency, in hertz (Hz)
Mms: the total moving mass (cone, coil and the air load moving with them), in kilograms (kg)
Cms: the mechanical compliance of the suspension: how far it moves per newton of force, in metres per newton (m/N); higher compliance means a softer suspension
π: pi, about 3.14159
√: square root
kg: kilogram, the unit of mass
m: metre, the unit of length
N: newton, the unit of force
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: Like any mass on a spring, the resonance falls as the moving mass or the suspension's softness rises; four times the mass halves the resonance frequency.
```

### Qts: how damped the resonance is

Two things damp the resonance. The suspension loses some energy as heat (the mechanical Q, **Qms**). The voice coil moving in the magnet generates a voltage that the amplifier's low output impedance loads through a low-resistance circuit, which brakes the cone (the electrical Q, **Qes**). They combine like resistors in parallel, so the total is always lower than either part and the smaller one dominates:

```formula reference
Qts = (Qms Qes) / (Qms + Qes)
where
Qts: the total Q of the driver at Fs (no unit); lower means more damped
Qms: the mechanical Q, set by losses in the suspension (no unit); typically several, e.g. 4
Qes: the electrical Q, set by braking from the motor and amplifier (no unit); typically 0.2 to 1, e.g. 0.4
In words: Mechanical and electrical damping combine like resistors in parallel, so the total Q is below both and is dominated by the smaller one, usually the electrical Q.
```

With a mechanical Q of 4 and an electrical Q of 0.4, the total Q is about 0.36, close to the electrical Q. That is typical: the motor does most of the damping. Q has no unit because it is a ratio (stored energy to energy lost per cycle, roughly).

### Vas: the suspension expressed as air

Vas turns the suspension's springiness into "the volume of air that would be just as springy" under the same cone. It grows with the suspension's compliance and with the **square of the cone area**: doubling the cone area quadruples Vas. A roughly 8-inch woofer (about 0.022 m² of cone) with a 1 mm/N suspension has a Vas of about 68 litres.

So for a fixed cone area, larger Vas means a softer suspension. Because Vas grows with cone area squared, it is not a stiffness comparison across arbitrary driver sizes: a big woofer can have a large Vas with a stiff suspension.

Vas matters because it is compared with the box volume: a box much smaller than Vas has an air spring much stiffer than the suspension, so the box, not the driver, sets the system's resonance (next lesson). Factory tolerances are wide (Purdue's notes give about ±15 % on Fs and ±20–30 % on Vas), so measuring your own driver is worthwhile.

## Key takeaways
- Moving mass and suspension compliance determine free-air resonance.
- Mechanical and electrical damping combine into total Q.
- Equivalent compliance volume depends on both cone area and suspension compliance.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)

lessons.title: Estimate a sealed box’s resonance and Q
lessons.summary: Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide.
lessons.body:
## Driver choice and sealed-box alignment

### Efficiency bandwidth product

A rough first sort uses the **efficiency bandwidth product** (EBP): the free-air resonance divided by the electrical Q. Purdue's rule of thumb is that drivers with an EBP around 50 tend to suit sealed boxes and those around 100 suit ported ones. A driver with a high resonance and a strong motor (low electrical Q) therefore leans towards ported. It's a starting point, not a design method: always model the full parameter set.

```formula reference
EBP = Fs / Qes
where
EBP: the efficiency bandwidth product, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz)
Qes: the electrical Q (no unit)
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: Divide the free-air resonance by the electrical Q; values around 50 suggest a sealed box and around 100 a ported one, as a first guess only.
```

Manufacturing tolerances are loose: Purdue's notes give typical factory tolerances of about ±15% for Fs and ±20–30% for Vas. Measure your own driver if accuracy matters.

### The sealed-box relationships

Put a driver in a sealed box. The air trapped in the box is a second spring pushing on the cone, alongside the suspension. A smaller box is a stiffer spring. The **compliance ratio** says how stiff the box air is compared with the suspension, and both the resonance and its Q rise with the square root of the total stiffness. These closed-box results (Small, 1972) are the core of choosing a box size:

```formula reference
α = Vas / Vb
Fc = Fs √(1 + α)
Qtc = Qts √(1 + α)
where
α: alpha, the compliance ratio (no unit): how many times stiffer the box air is than the driver's suspension
Vas: the driver's equivalent compliance volume, in litres (L)
Vb: the internal volume of the box, in litres (L)
Fc: the resonance frequency of the driver in the box, in hertz (Hz)
Fs: the driver's free-air resonance, in hertz (Hz)
Qtc: the total Q of the driver in the box (no unit); it sets the shape of the bass roll-off
Qts: the driver's total Q in free air (no unit)
√: square root
L: litre, a unit of volume; 1 L = 0.001 m^3
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: The smaller the box compared with the driver's Vas, the stiffer the trapped air, and the more the resonance and the Q in the box both rise above the driver's free-air values, by the same factor.
```

The important consequence is that **resonance and Q move together**. You cannot make a sealed box smaller without also raising its resonance and making it peakier, and a bigger box gives lower, more damped bass. These relationships ignore box losses and stuffing, and they assume the box is small compared with the wavelength (true in the bass).

The sealed-box **total Q** sets the shape of the bass roll-off. The box-and-driver is a second-order high-pass filter, and the level exactly at Fc depends only on Qtc:

| Qtc | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| 0.5 | Critically damped, −6 dB at Fc |
| 0.707 | Butterworth: maximally flat, −3 dB at Fc |
| ~1.0–1.1 | Peak before roll-off, "boomier" |

For example, take a driver with a 30 Hz free-air resonance, total Q of 0.35 and a 60 L equivalent compliance volume:

| Box | Fc | Qtc | Character |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 L | about 79 Hz | about 0.93 | peaky, less deep |
| 20 L | 60 Hz | 0.70 | near-Butterworth |
| 40 L | about 47 Hz | about 0.55 | deeper, well damped |

Deep bass extension, reference efficiency and enclosure volume are coupled. “Pick two” summarizes the trade-off; real driver excursion, losses and power limits still constrain the design.

(Filling the box with absorbent material can make it behave as if it were somewhat larger: Purdue's notes say up to about 15% in apparent volume, while also adding some effective moving mass.)

## Key takeaways
- Efficiency bandwidth product is only an initial enclosure-selection guide.
- A smaller sealed box raises both resonance and Q in the ideal model.
- Real losses, stuffing and measured driver parameters affect the finished alignment.

## Further reading
- [Loudspeaker parameters — D. G. Meyer, Purdue](https://engineering.purdue.edu/ece103/LectureNotes/SRS_Loudspeaker_Parameters.pdf)
- [Helmholtz resonance — Joe Wolfe, UNSW](https://phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Helmholtz.html)
- [Monopole and dipole radiation — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/rad2/mdq.html)
