lessons.title: Follow a console channel and its sends
lessons.summary: Each system stage has noise and overload limits.
lessons.body:
Up to now we've looked at parts: microphones, drivers, boxes, crossovers, amplifiers. A **sound system** connects them so that a source (your synth, a voice, a drum) reaches listeners at the right level, with the right balance and without noise, distortion or feedback. Whether it's a desk in your bedroom or a festival PA, the principles are the same.

## The chain

```flow
Source: synth, mic or instrument
DI box or mic: to balanced mic/line level
Console: preamp gain, EQ, routing, mix
Processing: system EQ, delay, crossover
Power amplifiers (or powered speakers)
Loudspeakers
Room and listeners
```

Every stage has a **noise floor** below the signal and a **clipping point** above it. The job is to keep the signal comfortably between them at every stage.

## The mixing console

A console (mixer, desk) combines many inputs into a few outputs, with independent control over each. Digital consoles and DAWs (Ableton's mixer included) copy the analogue layout, so learning one teaches you the others.

### The channel strip

Signal flows from top to bottom of a typical channel:

1. **Input and preamp gain (trim).** Brings mic or line level up to the console's internal operating level. This is the most important control on the desk for noise and headroom. Phantom power and a pad switch usually live here.
2. **High-pass filter.** Removes rumble and handling noise below the useful range of the source. Engage it only where removing those frequencies suits the source and the intended sound.
3. **Insert point.** A send and return that loops the channel's signal out to an external processor (a compressor, say) and back, in series.
4. **EQ.** Shelving and parametric bands for tone and to make room for other sources.
5. **Dynamics processing** (on many digital desks): gate and compressor.
6. **Aux sends.** Copies of the channel at an adjustable level to separate **aux buses**, used for monitor mixes and effects.
   - **Pre-fader** sends ignore the channel fader: right for **monitor mixes**, so the front-of-house engineer's fader moves don't change what the performer hears.
   - **Post-fader** sends follow the fader: right for effects like reverb, so the wet signal fades with the dry.
7. **Panning** places the signal in the stereo bus.
8. **Fader** sets the channel's level in the mix.
9. **Signal routing** assigns the channel to the main mix and/or **subgroups**.

### Buses and subgroups

A **mix bus** is any point where signals are summed. The main L/R mix is a bus; so are aux sends and subgroups.

- **Subgroups** sum related channels (all drums, all backing vocals) to one fader, so you can ride a whole section, or compress it together, with one control.
- **VCA or DCA groups** (on many consoles) are a variation: one fader remotely controls the faders of its member channels without summing audio.

## Key takeaways
- Each system stage has noise and overload limits.
- Pre-fader sends can keep monitor mixes independent of channel fader moves.
- Subgroups sum audio; VCA and DCA groups control channel gains.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: Which kind of aux send should feed a performer's monitor wedge, and why?

options.text: Pre-fader, so the monitor mix is independent of the channel fader
options.explanation: Correct. Monitor mixes use pre-fader sends.

options.text: Post-fader, so monitors follow the front-of-house mix
options.explanation: Then every FOH fader move would change what the performer hears, which is distracting and can cause feedback.

options.text: The insert send
options.explanation: Inserts loop the channel through a processor in series; they're not mix sends.

options.text: The main L/R bus

- **Pre-fader**: taps the signal before the channel fader. Used for monitors.
- **Post-fader**: follows the fader. Used for effects (reverb, delay) so wet and dry stay balanced.

The FOH engineer can then mix freely without changing the stage sound.

options.text: Post-fader, so the reverb level follows the vocal fader
options.explanation: Correct. The wet/dry balance stays constant as you ride the vocal.

options.text: Pre-fader, so the reverb stays at a constant level
options.explanation: Then pulling the vocal fader down leaves the reverb behind on its own.

lessons.title: Plan gain across the whole system
lessons.summary: Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom.
lessons.body:
## Gain staging across the system

Module 1 covered gain staging inside a digital synth. In a system, the same idea applies at every box:

1. **Set the preamp gain first**, with the performer at their loudest. Aim for healthy levels with headroom to spare: on a digital desk, nominal levels around −18 to −20 dBFS leave room for peaks (module 1); on an analogue desk, follow its meter calibration and overload-warning guidance, allowing headroom for unexpectedly loud peaks rather than deliberately clipping. The system's signal-to-noise ratio is largely fixed here: noise added at the mic preamp is amplified by everything after it.
2. **Keep faders near their unity (0 dB) mark** for normal levels, so there's travel in both directions.
3. **Set outboard gear to unity** where possible, passing the full signal without clipping.
4. **Set amplifier input sensitivity** as part of the system’s gain and protection plan. One approach maps the maximum clean system output to the required amplifier output; that output must also respect speaker and audience limits. Amp input controls are attenuators that set sensitivity, not "power" controls.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: photocopying a pencil sketch
> Photocopy a faint pencil sketch, then copy the copy several times, darkening each one to make the lines visible. Every copier adds its own speckle, and darkening a faint copy darkens the speckle just as much. Start with a firm, dark original and the speckle stays insignificant; press so hard that the lines smudge into solid black, though, and no later copy can recover the detail.
>
> **How it maps:** The sketch is the source signal, each copier is a stage in the chain, and the speckle is each stage's noise. Setting a healthy preamp gain is drawing a firm original. Turning a faint signal up later (faders at the top) darkens the speckle too. Smudged solid black is clipping, which no later stage can undo.
>
> **Where it stops:** Digital stages add almost no noise of their own once the signal is converted, and an analogue chain's noise depends on each stage's design. The analogy also hides headroom: a real chain needs space above the normal level for unexpectedly loud peaks.

How much preamp gain does a mic need? Start from its sensitivity (its output at 1 pascal, which is 94 dB SPL), then add one decibel of output for every decibel the real source is above that reference. The preamp makes up the gap to the console's working level. Every decibel louder at the mic means one decibel less preamp gain.

For example, an SM58 (sensitivity −56.0 dBV/Pa) on a singer producing 104 dB SPL, 10 dB above 1 Pa, puts out about −46 dBV, which is about −44 dBu (dBu reads about 2.2 dB higher than dBV for the same voltage). Reaching a +4 dBu working level therefore takes about **48 dB** of preamp gain. A condenser about 25 dB more sensitive (the microphone lessons) would need only around 23 dB.

> [!warning] Two common mistakes
> - Low preamp gain "made up" with faders pushed to the top: the console's noise is amplified as much as the signal.
> - Preamp gain set with the singer warming up quietly: the first chorus clips the input, and no fader can undo clipping that happened upstream.

## Key takeaways
- Set input gain with representative source peaks and leave headroom.
- A fader cannot repair clipping at an earlier stage.
- Coordinate amplifier sensitivity, limiter settings and speaker and audience limits.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

questions.prompt: On a console channel, which control most affects the channel's noise and headroom?

options.text: The channel fader
options.explanation: The fader comes after the preamp; it can't fix a signal that's too quiet or clipped at the input.

options.text: The pan control
options.explanation: Pan only distributes the signal between left and right.

options.text: The aux send
options.explanation: Sends only affect the copies sent to aux buses.

options.text: The preamp gain (trim)
options.explanation: Correct. It sets the level everything after it works with; noise added here is amplified by everything downstream.

questions.workedExample: RaneNote 135: take as much gain as practical at the mic stage, because the system's signal-to-noise ratio is largely fixed there. Then keep faders near unity.

questions.prompt: An SM58 on a singer producing 104 dB SPL at the mic needs about 48 dB of preamp gain to reach the console's +4 dBu working level. You move the same SM58 to a guitar cabinet that produces 114 dB SPL at the mic. Roughly how much preamp gain does it need now?

options.text: About 58 dB
options.explanation: That gets the direction backwards. A louder source gives more output from the mic, so it needs less gain.

options.text: About 48 dB: the mic has not changed
options.explanation: The mic's sensitivity is the same, but its output rises one decibel for every decibel of extra sound pressure.

options.text: About 38 dB
options.explanation: Correct. The cabinet is 10 dB louder at the mic, so the mic puts out 10 dB more and the preamp needs about 10 dB less gain.

options.text: About 4 dB
options.explanation: The mic output is still far below line level; 10 dB louder does not close a 48 dB gap.

questions.workedExample:
1. Mic output rises decibel for decibel with the sound pressure at the mic, because the mic is linear in that range.
2. 114 dB SPL is 10 dB above 104 dB SPL, so the SM58 puts out about 10 dB more voltage.
3. The console's target level is unchanged, so the preamp must make up 10 dB less: about 48 − 10 = 38 dB.

Set gain with the source at its loudest, leaving headroom, because a fader cannot undo clipping at the preamp.

questions.prompt: The console has a maximum clean sine-wave output of +18 dBu RMS. The power amp reaches its rated maximum clean sine output at +5.1 dBu RMS with input attenuation at zero. Assume no limiter. How do these gain limits compare?

options.text: None: more headroom at the console is always better
options.explanation: The issue is the amp: it reaches full power long before the console approaches its own limit.

options.text: The amplifier reaches its clean-output limit about 13 dB before the console reaches its own limit
options.explanation: Correct. About 13 dB of input attenuation would align those stated limits; the actual system may need a lower target output and suitable protection.

options.text: The speakers will be too quiet
options.explanation: They'll be loud; the problem is clipping and tweeter risk.

options.text: The console will clip before the amp
options.explanation: The console has about 13 dB more range than the amp needs.

questions.workedExample:
1. Put both limits in the same unit: the console can output up to +18 dBu cleanly; the amplifier reaches full clean power at +5.1 dBu in.
2. The console therefore has about 13 dB more range than the amplifier can use: the amp runs out of clean power about 13 dB before the console does.
3. About 13 dB of amplifier input attenuation would align those clean sine-wave limits, so the console's full range maps onto the amp's full range.

Music peak metering, limiter thresholds, speaker limits and audience exposure still need separate consideration, and the target may be a lower maximum output.

lessons.title: Connect an instrument through a DI
lessons.summary: A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input.
lessons.body:
## DI boxes

A **DI (direct input) box** connects an instrument or line-level source to a console's balanced **mic input**:

- It accepts an instrument or line-level signal and provides a **low-impedance, balanced, mic-level** output. Passive guitar pickups often need a high input impedance; synth and keyboard line outputs are usually low impedance and may already be balanced. Choose the DI or direct line connection to suit both devices.
- That lets the signal travel down a long multicore to the desk with good noise rejection (module 5's balanced lines).
- Most DIs have a **ground lift** switch to break a ground loop between stage gear and the desk's ground (module 3), and many have a pad.

Two types:

- **Passive DIs** use a transformer. No power needed; robust; the transformer gives galvanic isolation.
- **Active DIs** use a buffer amplifier, powered by phantom power or a battery. They load high-impedance sources (like passive guitar pickups) very lightly.

For your synth on a stage, a DI is usually the right way into a PA, with the synth's output at line level into the DI's input (use its pad if needed).

## Key takeaways
- A suitable DI provides balanced mic-level output for a microphone input.
- Select its input impedance and pad for the actual source.
- A compatible balanced line connection may remove the need for a DI.

lessons.title: Audience coverage and delay alignment
lessons.summary: Main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs.
lessons.body:
## PA design

A typical live PA has several systems, each with its own job:

- **Main speakers (front of house).** Left/right or mono speakers covering the audience, flown or on stands. Larger venues use **line arrays**: vertical columns of boxes that control vertical coverage and lose level more slowly with distance over part of their range.
- **Subwoofers.** Below about 80–120 Hz. Usually on the ground. Several subs can be arranged (end-fire, cardioid, arc) to steer low frequencies away from the stage.
- **Stage monitor loudspeakers.** What performers hear: **floor wedges** aimed up at each performer, side fills, or **in-ear monitors (IEMs)**. Fed from **pre-fader aux** mixes.
- **Front fills.** Small speakers along the stage lip for the front rows, who are below the main speakers' coverage.
- **Delay speakers.** Further back in large venues, where the main speakers have lost too much level.

### Delay speakers

At a chosen listener position, compare the path from the main speaker with the path from the delay speaker. Sound from the main speakers has further to travel, so without an electronic delay the delay speaker's copy would arrive first and pull the sound image towards it (the precedence effect, from the hearing lessons). The delay to dial in is:

- the **extra travel time** of the main speakers' sound: about 2.9 ms per metre of extra path, so a 40 m longer path is about 117 ms;
- **plus the difference in processing latency** between the two paths (main path minus delay path). If that would make the total negative, change the other path or the design instead.

The alignment holds exactly only where the path difference is the one you designed for. Behind the delay speaker, on the straight line from the main speakers through it, moving further back adds the same distance to both paths, so the difference, and the alignment, stay the same. Off that line, and especially between the stage and the delay speaker, the difference changes: there the delay speaker's sound arrives late and can be heard as an echo. This is why delay speakers are aimed away from the stage and cover only the area behind them.

A designer may choose an additional offset to favour the main speakers as the first arrival, but no universal 10–20 ms setting guarantees fusion or stage localisation. Those depend on signal, relative level, geometry and reflections; measure and listen throughout the overlap region.

## Studio vs live

| | Studio | Live |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | Accurate monitoring | Coverage, level |
| Listeners | One position | Whole audience |
| Speakers | Near-field monitors | PA, subs, wedges |
| Feedback | Rarely an issue | Constant concern |
| Room | Treated (the room-acoustics units) | Take what you get |

In a studio the monitors must tell the truth, so you can make decisions that translate to other systems. In a live system the goal is even, intelligible, sufficiently loud coverage for everyone, with controlled exposure and compliance with applicable venue limits. WHO’s 100 dB LAeq,15 min ceiling is one part of its safe-listening venue standard, not a guarantee that a whole event is safe at that level (the hearing units).

## Key takeaways
- Main speakers, subs, fills, delays and monitors serve different coverage needs.
- Align a fill using acoustic-path and processing-latency differences.
- Verify timing, localisation, overlap and exposure throughout the audience area.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)

lessons.title: Improve gain before acoustic feedback
lessons.summary: Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain.
lessons.body:
## Acoustic feedback

**Acoustic feedback** happens when the sound from a speaker re-enters a microphone, is amplified, comes out of the speaker louder, and so on. Sustained feedback can develop where the **loop gain** magnitude reaches or exceeds one (0 dB) and the phase reinforces the circulating signal. The precise stability and onset depend on the whole loop. Feedback develops at a frequency where both loop magnitude and reinforcing phase conditions are met: often a peak in a speaker's or mic's response, or a room resonance.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: two facing mirrors
> Stand between two mirrors facing each other and you see a corridor of reflections, each a little dimmer than the last, fading away. Imagine instead that each mirror made the image slightly *brighter* every time it bounced: the corridor would blaze up until something saturated.
>
> **How it maps:** One trip round the loop, from speaker through the air into the mic and back out of the speaker, is one bounce. Ordinary mirrors are a loop gain below one: each pass is quieter and the sound dies away (the system "rings" briefly when close). An amplifying mirror is a loop gain at or above one with reinforcing phase: each pass is louder and the howl builds until something clips.
>
> **Where it stops:** Real feedback happens at particular frequencies where the phase round the loop reinforces, not at all frequencies at once, and the loop includes the room's reflections. Mirrors also have no equivalent of EQ: in a sound system you can cut the gain at just the frequency that rings.

How to get more **gain before feedback**:

1. **Get the mic close to the source.** Halving the source-to-mic distance gives about 6 dB more source level at the mic (inverse square law), so 6 dB less gain is needed.
2. **Keep speakers away from mics**, and put main speakers in front of the mic line.
3. **Use directional mics and their nulls.** Put wedges in the null of the mic's pattern (the microphone units).
4. **Fewer open mics.** In the usual approximate potential-acoustic-gain model, doubling similarly coupled **open microphones (NOM)** costs about 3 dB; actual loop paths can differ. Mute what isn't in use.
5. **EQ.** "Ringing out" the system: raise gain until it starts to ring, identify the frequency, and cut it by a few dB with a parametric EQ band. RaneNote 158 warns that very narrow, deep notches cope poorly when temperature or positions change, and favours shallow cuts of moderate width. Automatic notch-based feedback suppressors do this live, but they typically add only a couple of dB of margin.
6. **In-ear monitors** remove the wedge-to-mic path when wedges are actually removed from that mix.

The 6 dB figure in step 1 comes from the inverse square law: every halving of the source-to-mic distance gives about 6 dB more source level at the mic, so the channel needs 6 dB less gain for the same output. Very close to a directional mic, the proximity effect also boosts the bass, and a voice is not a point source, so treat 6 dB per halving as a guide.

The 3 dB figure in step 4 comes from the potential acoustic gain (PAG) model. Each open mic picks up some of the PA, and the model treats those similarly coupled pickups as unrelated signals, which add in power: twice as many open mics is about +3 dB of PA in the mix (like two unrelated sources in the acoustics lessons), so each halving of the number of open mics buys back about 3 dB. Real stages differ: mics nearer a wedge contribute more than the model assumes.

## Key takeaways
- Feedback depends on reinforcing loop phase as well as gain.
- Improve source pickup while reducing loudspeaker pickup at microphones.
- The open-microphone count rule is an approximation; geometry and individual coupling matter.

## Further reading
- [Setting system level controls — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note135.html)
- [Acoustic feedback — Rane](https://www.ranecommercial.com/legacy/note158.html)
- [Keyboard stage connections — Radial](https://www.radialeng.com/blog/how-to-manage-any-keyboard-setup-on-stage)

lessons.title: Predict rectangular-room mode frequencies
lessons.summary: Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families.
lessons.body:
Put the best monitors in the world in an untreated, square, bare-walled room and you'll hear the room as much as the speakers. Below a few hundred hertz, a small room's response at your listening position can swing by 20 dB or more between neighbouring frequencies. Mix there and you'll correct for problems that only exist in your room, and the mix will sound wrong everywhere else.

This lesson is about understanding what a room does, then placing monitors and treatment so you can trust what you hear.

## Room modes

Between two parallel walls, a sound wave reflects back and forth. At frequencies where a whole number of half-wavelengths fits exactly between the walls, the reflections reinforce each other into a **standing wave**: a **room mode** (or resonance).

The rule that one half-wavelength, two half-wavelengths, three and so on must fit the gap exactly, combined with the link between wavelength and frequency, gives the mode frequencies between one pair of walls:

```formula essential
f_n = nc / (2L)
where
f_n: the frequency of the nth mode between this pair of walls, in hertz (Hz)
n: the mode number, a whole number 1, 2, 3 …; mode 1 is the lowest (fundamental), mode 2 is twice its frequency, and so on
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s) at 20 °C
L: the distance between the two parallel walls, in metres (m)
In words: the lowest mode is the frequency whose half-wavelength exactly spans the gap between the walls, and every whole-number multiple of it is a mode too. The bigger the room, the lower the modes.
```

For two walls 5.0 m apart, the first mode is about 34 Hz, the second about 69 Hz and the third about 103 Hz: whole-number multiples of the first, not equal steps from an arbitrary start. Halve the spacing and every mode doubles in frequency. The relationship assumes rigid, parallel, flat walls; real walls flex and absorb a little, which damps and slightly shifts the modes.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a skipping rope
> Two people turning a long skipping rope can make it swing in one big loop, or, turning faster, in two loops with a still point in the middle, or three. In between those rhythms the rope just flails without settling into a steady shape.
>
> **How it maps:** The rope's length is the distance between the walls. Each steady shape is a mode: one loop is the first mode (half a wavelength across the gap), two loops the second, and so on, at whole-number multiples of the slowest rhythm. The still points are the nodes.
>
> **Where it stops:** The rope is held still at its ends, whereas sound pressure is at its *maximum* at a rigid wall. And a room is three-dimensional, so modes also form across the width, the height and diagonally, all at once.

Those are **axial modes**: between one pair of surfaces. They usually carry the most energy and have the greatest influence on the low-frequency response. **Tangential modes** involve two pairs of surfaces and **oblique modes** all three. For a rectangular (shoebox) room, one relationship covers all three kinds; exclude the all-zero combination, which is static pressure rather than an oscillating acoustic mode:

```formula reference
f = (c / 2) √((n_x / L_x)^2
    + (n_y / L_y)^2 + (n_z / L_z)^2)
where
f: the frequency of the mode, in hertz (Hz)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
√: the square root of everything inside the brackets that follow it
n_x: the mode number along the length: 0, 1, 2 … (0 means the mode doesn't involve that pair of walls)
n_y: the mode number along the width: 0, 1, 2 …
n_z: the mode number along the height: 0, 1, 2 …
L_x: the room's length, in metres (m)
L_y: the room's width, in metres (m)
L_z: the room's height, in metres (m)
In words: Each rectangular-room mode is labelled by three whole numbers counting half-wavelengths along the length, width and height; one non-zero number gives an axial mode, two a tangential mode and three an oblique mode.
```

A tangential mode always sits higher than the axial modes it combines. For a 5.0 × 3.6 m floor plan, the axial modes along the length and width are about 34 Hz and 48 Hz, and the tangential mode combining them is about 59 Hz. Like the axial relationship, this assumes rigid walls and a perfectly rectangular room.

## Key takeaways
- Ideal rectangular rigid rooms have axial, tangential and oblique mode families.
- Mode frequency depends on room dimensions and mode numbers.
- Wall flexibility and absorption modify the ideal result.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)
- [Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/rt60/rt60.html)
- [REW help — Room EQ Wizard](https://www.roomeqwizard.com/help/help_en-GB/html/index.html)

lessons.title: Relate modal frequencies to room position
lessons.summary: Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat.
lessons.body:
## Room dimensions and listener position

### An example room

A small studio of 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m. Each dimension has its own series of axial modes, whole-number multiples of its lowest one (the previous lesson):

| Dimension | First three axial modes |
|---|---|
| Length 5.0 m | 34.3, 68.6, 102.9 Hz |
| Width 3.6 m | 47.6, 95.3, 142.9 Hz |
| Height 2.4 m | 71.5, 142.9, 214.4 Hz |

Notice that 3.6 ÷ 2.4 = 1.5, so the width's third mode and the height's second land on the **same frequency, 142.9 Hz**. Coincident modal frequencies can produce strong response peaks, depending on how the sources excite them, the listener position and damping. Rooms whose dimensions are simple multiples of each other (a cube has particularly extensive degeneracy) bunch their modes; unrelated dimensions spread them out more evenly.

What a mode does at your seat depends on **where you sit**:

- For ideal rigid rectangular boundaries, each axial mode has pressure antinodes at its corresponding pair of walls. A general mode may still have nodes along other coordinates on a wall; corners are pressure antinodes of all these ideal modes.
- The first axial mode has a **pressure null** halfway between its walls. At the length midpoint, that ideal mode contributes no pressure; moving away can increase its contribution. The total response also contains direct sound and other modes, so it is not necessarily silent or boomy.
- So bass response varies dramatically with position. This is why many guides suggest avoiding the exact centre of the room for the listening position (Genelec suggests sitting in the front part of the room for music work, and at least 1 m from walls).

## Key takeaways
- Coincident modal frequencies do not alone predict the response at a particular seat.
- Source excitation, damping and listener position all matter.
- Avoid treating a node of one mode as silence in the total sound field.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)

lessons.title: Estimate decay with Sabine’s equation
lessons.summary: Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay.
lessons.body:
## Reverberation and RT60

After a sound stops, its reflections take time to die away. **RT60** is the time for the sound level to fall by **60 dB**. Wallace Sabine's empirical equation (from experiments at Harvard around 1900) relates it to the room's volume and absorption. Use it to estimate how live a room will sound, and how much treatment you'd need to change that:

```formula reference
RT60 = 0.161V / A
A = Σ (S_i α_i)
where
RT60: the reverberation time, in seconds (s): how long the sound takes to fall by 60 decibels (dB) after the source stops
0.161: Sabine's constant for metric units, in seconds per metre (s/m); it comes from 24 × ln(10) ÷ 343 ≈ 0.161, where 343 m/s is the speed of sound
V: the room's volume, in cubic metres (m³)
A: the room's total absorption, in square metres (m²), also called metric sabins: the area of open window that would absorb the same amount
Σ: sigma, "add up the following for every surface"
i: a counter that runs over the room's surfaces (walls, floor, ceiling, panels)
S_i: the area of surface i, in square metres (m²)
α_i: alpha, the absorption coefficient of surface i: the effective fraction of incident energy not returned by that surface at the frequency considered, from 0 (perfect reflector) to 1 (perfect absorber)
In words: reverberation time grows with the room's volume and shrinks with how much absorbing surface it contains. Double the absorption and you halve RT60.
```

The total equivalent absorption area is each surface area multiplied by its frequency-dependent absorption coefficient, summed. The relationship has two levers, and the second is usually the only practical one:

- **Volume.** A bigger room, with the same surfaces, takes longer to die away.
- **Absorption.** Doubling the total absorption halves the reverberation time. Because hard surfaces absorb so little, a modest area of effective absorbers can dominate the total.

For example, a 5.0 × 3.6 × 2.4 m studio (43.2 m³, about 77 m² of surface) with bare surfaces averaging an absorption coefficient of 0.10 has about 7.7 m² of absorption and an RT60 of about 0.9 s. Swap 10 m² of that surface for panels with a coefficient of 0.90 and the absorption roughly doubles, to about 15.7 m²: the RT60 falls to about 0.44 s. Ten square metres of panels, about an eighth of the surface, halved the decay time.

> [!analogy] Real-world analogy: a bath and its plughole
> Pull the plug on a full bath and it drains at a rate set by the size of the plughole. A bigger bath takes longer to empty through the same plughole; a second plughole empties it twice as fast.
>
> **How it maps:** The water is the sound energy left in the room after the source stops. The bath's size is the room's volume, and the plugholes are its absorption: each absorbing surface is another hole letting energy out. Double the absorption and the room "drains" in half the time.
>
> **Where it stops:** A bath empties at a roughly steady rate, whereas sound energy dies away by the same *fraction* in each moment, so its level falls steadily in decibels. And a room's plugholes change size with frequency: panels that drain the treble quickly may barely touch the bass.

Two caveats:

- **Absorption coefficients depend on frequency.** A treatment that works at 2 kHz may do almost nothing at 100 Hz, so RT60 is quoted per octave band, and a room can be dead in the treble while still booming in the bass.
- **Sabine assumes a fairly live room with diffuse sound.** At higher broadly distributed absorption a diffuse-field Eyring model can improve the estimate; neither model is guaranteed for a strongly non-diffuse room, and in small rooms below the Schroeder frequency "reverberation time" is a rough description at best.

Control rooms are typically much drier than living rooms; recommended targets vary by standard and room size, so treat any single number as a guide.

## Key takeaways
- Reverberation time describes a sixty-decibel decay.
- Sabine’s model uses room volume and equivalent absorption area.
- The diffuse-field and absorption assumptions limit its use, especially in small rooms.

lessons.title: Modal transition, absorption and diffusion
lessons.summary: The Schroeder estimate marks a gradual transition rather than a sharp frequency boundary.
lessons.body:
## The modal-to-statistical transition

### The Schroeder frequency

At low frequencies, modes are few and far apart, and the room behaves like a set of resonances. Higher up, modes overlap so densely that the room behaves statistically, as reverberation. The crossover between the two is often estimated by the **Schroeder frequency**. It needs the room's volume and its reverberation time (RT60, the time sound takes to die away by 60 dB, defined in the reverberation lesson). Small rooms and long reverberation times push it up:

```formula reference
f_S ≈ 2000 √(RT60 / V)
where
f_S: the Schroeder frequency, in hertz (Hz): roughly where the room stops acting like separate resonances and starts acting like a smooth reverberant space
≈: approximately equal to; this is a rule-of-thumb estimate, not an exact boundary
2000: a constant that follows from Schroeder's criterion that about three neighbouring modes overlap within each mode's bandwidth (a threshold he chose from measurement experience); it assumes RT60 in seconds and V in cubic metres
√: the square root of the bracket that follows
RT60: the reverberation time, in seconds (s)
V: the room's volume, in cubic metres (m³)
In words: The Schroeder estimate rises with reverberation time and falls with room volume, so a small studio has a wide band of troublesome modal bass, while a large hall's transition sits much lower.
```

For the treated 43.2 m³ studio from the reverberation lesson, with an RT60 of 0.44 s, the estimate is about 200 Hz: below that, the room behaves as separate modes. A large hall can sit far lower, although it can still have audible low-frequency problems.

The transition is gradual, not a sharp line.

Below it, think **room modes** (fix with placement and bass traps). Above it, think **sound reflections** and **reverberation** (fix with absorption and diffusion).

## Absorption vs diffusion

- **Absorbers** convert sound energy to heat. **Porous absorbers** (mineral wool, fibreglass, thick acoustic foam) work by friction as air moves through them. They're most effective where the air particle velocity is high, which is about a **quarter wavelength from a hard wall**. A thin porous panel against a rigid wall generally absorbs low frequencies poorly (the quarter-wavelength rule below shows why). An air gap can improve lower-frequency absorption.
- **Diffusers** scatter sound in many directions without removing much energy. They break up strong specular reflections and flutter echo (rapid repeats between parallel hard walls) while keeping the room feeling live. They need to be large compared with the wavelengths they diffuse, so they work mainly in the mids and highs, and need some distance from the listener.

A good control room usually combines both: absorption where early reflections hit, diffusion or a mix at the back, and bass trapping in the corners.

### The quarter-wavelength rule

For a normally incident plane wave reflected from an ideal rigid wall, the air's particle velocity is zero at the wall and greatest a quarter wavelength away. A porous layer works best where the air moves, so the depth of the material (or of the air gap behind it) roughly sets the lowest frequency it reaches well: the frequency whose quarter wavelength fits between the wall and the material.

| Depth from wall | Frequency whose quarter wavelength fits |
|---|---|
| 5 cm | about 1.7 kHz |
| 10 cm | about 860 Hz |
| 1.4 m | about 60 Hz |

So a 10 cm panel corresponds to roughly 860 Hz, and reaching 60 Hz this way would need about 1.4 m: not practical. This is a rough guide, not a cut-off or a prediction of measured absorption: material flow resistance, thickness, mounting and the angle the sound arrives at all matter, oblique incidence changes the field, and a panel still absorbs something below this frequency.

### Bass traps

Bass wavelengths are metres long, so thin porous panels mounted against a rigid wall generally provide little bass absorption. Thin resonant panel systems are a different mechanism. **Bass traps** are:

- **Thick porous absorbers** (often 10–20 cm or more), commonly placed across **corners**. Straddling a corner leaves a large air gap behind the panel, which extends its effect to lower frequencies.
- **Pressure-based (membrane or Helmholtz) absorbers** tuned to specific low frequencies, which work by resonance and are most effective at pressure maxima such as walls and corners.

For the ideal rigid rectangular model, corners are pressure antinodes for all the mode families. In real rooms, boundaries and coupling differ. Treating them reduces the peaks and decay times of modes across the low end.

## Key takeaways
- The Schroeder estimate marks a gradual transition rather than a sharp frequency boundary.
- Porous absorption depends on thickness, mounting and material properties.
- Quarter-wavelength spacing is an intuition aid, not a hard absorption cutoff.
- Diffusers scatter energy; resonant bass absorbers use a different mechanism from porous panels.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)
- [Measured reverberation and Sabine’s equation — Dan Russell](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/demos/rt60/rt60.html)
- [REW help — Room EQ Wizard](https://www.roomeqwizard.com/help/help_en-GB/html/index.html)
- [Modal-overlap transition — Treble](https://docs.treble.tech/Transitionfrequency)
- [Acoustic treatment and boundary interference — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/improving-room-acoustics)

options.text: Foam perfectly reflects all frequencies regardless of thickness or mounting
options.explanation: Porous foam can absorb sound; this thin, rigid-wall-mounted layer simply provides little absorption at 60 Hz. Most unabsorbed energy is reflected by the assembly.

options.text: Bass is absorbed only by glass
options.explanation: Bass is absorbed by thick porous traps and by tuned membrane or Helmholtz absorbers.

options.text: 60 Hz is outside human hearing
options.explanation: 60 Hz is well within hearing.

options.text: Porous absorbers work where air particle velocity is high, about a quarter wavelength from the wall: at 60 Hz that's about 1.4 m
options.explanation: Correct. A thin panel flat on the wall sits where bass particle velocity is near zero.

questions.workedExample:
1. Porous absorbers turn sound into heat by friction as air moves through them, so they work best where the air moves fastest.
2. At a rigid wall the air's particle velocity is near zero; for normally incident sound it is greatest a quarter wavelength out.
3. At 60 Hz the wavelength is about 5.7 m, so that point is about 1.4 m from the wall, far beyond a 5 cm panel.

Bass traps are therefore thick, spaced off or straddling corners, or are pressure-based (membrane or Helmholtz) designs that work at the wall.

lessons.title: Place monitors and locate early reflections
lessons.summary: Use symmetrical stereo geometry and the speaker’s specified acoustic axis.
lessons.body:
## Early reflections and the mirror trick

The first reflections from the side walls, ceiling, desk and floor reach your ears a few milliseconds after the direct sound. Because they're close in time and level, they **comb-filter** with it (the acoustics units) and blur the stereo image.

**The mirror trick** finds where to put absorption:

1. Sit in the listening position.
2. Have someone slide a mirror flat along the side wall.
3. Wherever you can see a **monitor's tweeter** in the mirror, that's a first-reflection point. Mark it.
4. Repeat for the other wall and the ceiling (with a mirror on a pole, or a laser and some geometry).

Absorbers at those points reduce the strongest early reflections. The desk and the console surface are reflection points too, which is one reason monitors often go on stands behind the desk rather than on it.

## Near-field monitor placement

**Near-field monitors** are designed for short listening distances, often around 1–2 m, which increases direct sound relative to reflected sound. Actual room contribution still depends on the room, directivity and frequency. Placement guidelines, largely as Genelec's placement guide sets them out:

- **Equilateral triangle.** The two monitors and your head form an equilateral triangle: **60° between the monitors**, each aimed at the listening position.
- **Ear height.** The acoustic axis (usually between tweeter and woofer, or as the manual says) at ear level, typically 1.2–1.4 m from the floor for a seated listener. Tilt rather than lifting too high; Genelec suggests no more than about 15° of tilt.
- **Symmetry.** Place the setup symmetrically left–right in the room so both speakers see the same boundaries.
- **Avoid half room height and the room's exact middle**, where modes and floor-ceiling reflections line up badly.

```diagram
        L monitor      R monitor
            \   60 deg   /
             \          /
              \        /
               \      /
                listener
  (equal distances on all three sides)
```

## Key takeaways
- Use symmetrical stereo geometry and the speaker’s specified acoustic axis.
- The mirror method locates specular first-reflection paths.
- Listening distance alone does not remove the room’s contribution.

## Further reading
- [Monitor placement — Genelec](https://www.genelec.com/monitor-placement)
- [Driving room modes — Dan Russell, Penn State](https://www.acs.psu.edu/drussell/Demos/RoomModes/driving.html)

lessons.title: Diagnose boundary notches and measure the room
lessons.summary: A reflected path can cancel direct sound at particular frequencies.
lessons.body:
## Boundary interference

### Wall distance and SBIR

Sound radiates backwards from a monitor at low frequencies (it's omnidirectional there; the driver and enclosure units). That rear sound reflects off the front wall and returns. Where the reflected travel delays it by half a period, which happens when the distance to the wall is a **quarter wavelength**, it cancels the direct sound: **speaker boundary interference response (SBIR)**.

The reflected sound travels to the wall and back, an extra distance of twice the speaker-to-wall gap. The first cancellation happens when that extra distance is half a wavelength, so the wave comes back upside down. That puts the notch at the frequency whose quarter wavelength equals the gap: **move the speaker closer to the wall and the notch moves up in frequency**; move it further away and the notch moves down.

```formula reference
f_notch ≈ c / (4d)
where
f_notch: the frequency of the first (lowest) cancellation notch, in hertz (Hz)
d: the distance from the speaker's acoustic source to the wall behind it, in metres (m)
c: the speed of sound in air, about 343 metres per second (m/s)
≈: approximately equal to; this simple model only counts the straight-back-and-forth path
Hz: hertz, cycles per second
In words: The first boundary notch sits at the frequency whose quarter wavelength equals the speaker-to-wall distance, so halving the distance moves the notch up an octave.
```

This assumes the wall is rigid and the reflection travels straight back (the wall-perpendicular path). Real notches are shallower than a perfect cancellation and are partly filled by other paths. Typical distances:

| Speaker to front wall | First notch |
|---|---|
| 0.3 m | ≈ 286 Hz |
| 0.5 m | ≈ 172 Hz |
| 0.6 m | ≈ 143 Hz |
| 1.0 m | ≈ 86 Hz |

Genelec’s guide describes deep cancellation notches and advises against fixing them by boosting EQ. EQ scales both direct and reflected sound: a perfect null remains zero, while a finite dip can be raised locally only at the cost of headroom and potentially worse sound elsewhere. EQ does not remove the reflection or its geometry. Their remedies:

- **Flush-mount** the monitors in a hard wall, which removes the rear reflection.
- **Place them close to the wall**: typically with the front of the monitor less than 60 cm from the wall, so the notch moves up to frequencies where the speaker has already become forward-directing and sends less sound backwards, while leaving at least 5 cm clearance for a rear port.

A nearby wall also reinforces the bass below the notch (Genelec quotes about 6 dB for one close wall), so a monitor placed close to the wall or flush-mounted needs its low-frequency output turned down, for example with its room-response or bass-tilt controls.

The same cancellation happens with side walls, the floor and the desk at different distances, so varying those distances spreads the notches rather than stacking them.

## Measuring a room with REW

You can't fix what you can't measure, and ears are bad at judging bass in a room. **Room EQ Wizard (REW)** is free room-acoustics software for Windows, macOS and Linux. With a **calibrated measurement microphone** (for example a USB mic supplied with a calibration file), it:

- Plays a **swept sine** through your monitors and records it at the listening position.
- Computes the **impulse response**, and from it the **frequency response**, **waterfall plot** (how each frequency decays over time, which shows ringing modes clearly) and **decay / RT60** figures.
- Helps identify **room modes** and can calculate EQ filters.

A practical workflow:

1. Measure each monitor separately at the listening position, at a moderate level (the hearing units: protect your ears).
2. Look for big peaks and deep notches below about 300 Hz, and long decay in the waterfall.
3. Move the listening position and speakers first; that changes modes and SBIR far more than EQ can.
4. Add bass traps and first-reflection absorption, and re-measure.
5. Only then use EQ, mainly to **cut peaks**. Don't try to fill deep notches with boost: they're cancellations, and boosting them wastes amplifier power and driver excursion.

## Key takeaways
- A reflected path can cancel direct sound at particular frequencies.
- Placement and effective treatment change the reflection geometry; EQ does not remove it.
- Measure, change one cause and remeasure before applying final peak cuts.

## Further reading

questions.prompt: A monitor whose acoustic source is 0.4 m from a rigid front wall shows a deep first boundary (SBIR) notch at about 214 Hz. You move it so the source is 0.2 m from the wall. In the simple wall-reflection model, what happens to the notch?

options.text: It moves down an octave, to about 107 Hz
options.explanation: That is the direction for moving the speaker further away. A shorter round trip is half a wavelength of a shorter wave, which is a higher frequency.

options.text: It stays at 214 Hz, because the wall has not moved
options.explanation: The notch depends on the speaker-to-wall distance, which you changed.

options.text: It moves up an octave, to about 430 Hz, where the monitor radiates less sound backwards
options.explanation: Correct. Halving the distance halves the extra path, doubling the notch frequency. Higher up, the monitor is more directional, so less rear sound reaches the wall and the notch is usually shallower.

options.text: It disappears, because any distance under 0.5 m cancels nothing
options.explanation: A reflection still returns; moving close to the wall shifts the notch up to where less sound radiates backwards. Flush-mounting removes the rear reflection.

questions.workedExample:
1. Rear-radiated sound travels to the wall and back, an extra twice the gap. The first notch is where that extra path is half a wavelength: where the gap is a quarter wavelength.
2. Halving the gap halves the wavelength that fits, doubling the frequency: about 214 Hz to about 430 Hz.
3. Monitors become more directional as frequency rises, so less sound goes backwards there and the cancellation is usually shallower. That is why Genelec suggests placing monitors close to the front wall (or flush-mounting them), while keeping a rear port's clearance.

Do not try to fill these notches with EQ boost: it raises the reflection along with the direct sound.

questions.prompt: A measurement shows a deep dip near 120 Hz whose frequency changes when you move the monitor relative to the front wall. Which interpretation and first remedy best fit this evidence?

options.text: A room-mode peak: cut it with EQ
options.explanation: It is a dip, not a peak, and it moves with speaker-to-wall distance.

options.text: SBIR cancellation from the front wall; change the wall distance (closer or flush) or treat the wall rather than boosting
options.explanation: Correct. A notch near 120 Hz matches a speaker roughly 0.7 m from the wall, and its moving with wall distance points to that reflection. EQ boost raises the reflection as well as the direct sound.

options.text: The monitor's woofer is broken
options.explanation: A faulty woofer would not create a notch that moves with wall distance.

options.text: The microphone needs phantom power
options.explanation: Missing required power would prevent normal microphone operation; it does not explain a notch that tracks monitor-to-wall distance. Some measurement microphones use USB or other powering.

questions.workedExample:
1. The key evidence is that the dip moves when the monitor moves relative to the front wall: that points to a reflection from that wall.
2. A first SBIR notch sits where the speaker-to-wall gap is a quarter wavelength. At 120 Hz the wavelength is about 2.9 m, so the gap would be about 0.7 m: a very ordinary placement.
3. Remedies change the geometry: move the monitor much closer to the wall (pushing the notch up to where it radiates less backwards), flush-mount it, or reduce the reflection with effective treatment.
4. Boosting a finite dip can raise it at one point but consumes headroom and does not remove the reflection; a perfect cancellation remains a null. Re-measure after each change.

questions.prompt: After treating your room, REW shows a remaining 8 dB peak at 47 Hz and a deep, narrow 12 dB notch at 95 Hz at the listening position. How should you use EQ?

options.text: Cut the 47 Hz peak; leave the notch and address it with position changes instead
options.explanation: Correct. EQ is effective on modal peaks; deep notches are usually cancellations that EQ can't fill.

options.text: Boost 95 Hz by 12 dB and cut 47 Hz by 8 dB
options.explanation: Boosting a cancellation notch wastes amplifier power and driver excursion and usually doesn't fill it.

options.text: Don't use any EQ; it never helps rooms
options.explanation: Cutting modal peaks with EQ is a useful final step.

options.text: Boost everything below 100 Hz to compensate
options.explanation: That makes the 47 Hz peak worse.

questions.workedExample:
1. Peaks: excess energy at a mode. A parametric cut reduces it, but does not change the room mode’s physical damping or intrinsic decay time.
2. Notches: cancellation (a mode's null at your seat, or SBIR). Boosting scales direct and cancelling paths together. A finite dip can be raised locally but may require excessive headroom and worsen other seats; it does not remove the cancellation mechanism.
3. Fix notches by moving the seat or speakers, then re-measure.
